summary: BIOLOGICAL SAMPLE MICROSCALE ISOLATION AND ANTI-CROSS-CONTAMINATION AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:生物樣本微尺度隔離與防交叉污染極限 BIOLOGICAL SAMPLE MICROSCALE ISOLATION AND ANTI-CROSS-CONTAMINATION AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page, high-density English research monograph on whether microrobotic microscale isolation can improve sample-identity probability while limiting contact impulse, carryover and rare-sample loss. Its central claim is deliberately falsifiable. Under equal sample, time, energy, photon and analysis budgets, a preregistered isolation architecture should improve sample-identity probability without worsening contact impulse or carryover relative to commercial fluorescence-activated sorting at equal sample budget. A favorable result is rejected if downstream sensing creates the apparent improvement, rare targets silently disappear, purity rises by discarding difficult events, surface residue remains unresolved, or recovery improves while viability or molecular integrity fails. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates develop coverage entropy, calibrated identity posteriors, carryover transition models, complete material balance, rare-cell recovery and loss, purity, surface-memory decay, adsorption, desorption kinetics, hydrodynamic regime checks, contact impulse, shear dose, collision hazard, viability and molecular-integrity retention, blank limits, detection limits, witness information, uncertainty, equal-budget FACS effects, cross-site concordance and conjunctive release. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the book moves from identity authority and spatial coverage through contamination memory, microscale material closure, microrobotic contact physics, rare-cell accounting, decontamination, sample integrity, commercial FACS comparison and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates carry unique titles, questions, perturbations, rival accounts and evidence packets. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose genuinely different scientific objects, including contamination-memory ledgers, rare-cell censuses, adsorption compasses, waste-stream beacons, delayed-viability clocks and failure-preserving successor seeds. summary: Next-generation smart sensing devices necessitate on-chip integration of power-efficient reference circuits. The latters are required to provide other circuit blocks with highly reliable bias signals, even in the presence of temperature shifts and supply voltage disturbances, while draining a small fraction of the overall power budget. In particular, it is especially challenging to design current references with enhanced robustness and efficiency; hence, thorough exploration of novel architectures and design approaches is needed for this type of circuits. In this work, we propose a novel CMOS-only current reference, achieving temperature compensation by exploiting geometry dependences of the threshold voltage (specifically, the reverse short-channel effect and the narrow-channel effect). This allows reaching first-order temperature compensation within a single current reference core. Implemented in 0.18 μm CMOS, a version of the proposed current reference designed to deliver 141 nA (with 377 nW of total power consumption) achieved an average temperature coefficient equal to 194 ppm/°C (from −20 °C to 80 °C) and an average line sensitivity of −0.017%/V across post-layout statistical Monte Carlo simulations. Based on such findings, the newly proposed design methodology stands out as a noteworthy solution to design robust current references for power-constrained mixed-signal systems-on-chip.
title: A CMOS Current Reference with Novel Temperature Compensation Based on Geometry-Dependent Threshold Voltage Effects

summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.
title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks

summary: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a complex condition involving bidirectional interactions between cardiovascular and renal dysfunction. Its pathophysiology includes hemodynamic abnormalities, venous congestion, neurohormonal activation, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and metabolic disturbances. This narrative review aims to analyze the mechanisms of CRS and assess the relationship between renal function and clinical prognosis in patients with cardiovascular diseases, focusing on mortality, heart failure hospitalization, kidney dysfunction progression, and treatment-related renal changes. The review synthesizes evidence from clinical guidelines, randomized trials, observational studies, and contemporary scientific publications, with particular attention to CRS classification, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), serum creatinine, albuminuria, biomarkers, and treatment outcomes. The evidence indicates that reduced eGFR, albuminuria, persistent congestion, and worsening renal function provide complementary prognostic information. An analysis of 3,715 EVEREST trial participants found that each 30% decline in eGFR was associated with an increased risk of death and cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization. The DOSE trial showed that intensive diuretic treatment could improve fluid removal and symptoms while increasing short-term creatinine elevations. These findings highlight the importance of interpreting renal function changes alongside congestion, hemodynamic stability, baseline kidney function, and treatment response. Comprehensive cardiorenal risk assessment should incorporate renal function, albuminuria, urine output, cardiac biomarkers, electrolyte status, and clinical response to treatment. Further prospective studies are needed to validate integrated risk models in diverse patient populations.

title: CARDIORENAL SYNDROME IN CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN RENAL FUNCTION AND CLINICAL PROGNOSIS

summary: Abstract The lab for latent actors [ 1 ] proved its two-type results mostly on the complete pair cover of three or four variables. This companion asks the same questions for an arbitrary graph G of observed pairs on m binary variables. When do the pair tables admit a two-type explanation? Which freedoms remain? What does the set of explanations look like? Part I answers these at the pair layer. Existence ( theorem 2 ). A factorisation c ij = v i v j exists iff three conditions hold. No zero moment may join two variables that carry non-zero moments. On each component of the non-zero graph G ∗ , the sign cocycle must be a Z/2 coboundary, and log |c|must lie in the image of the unsigned incidence matrix. The last two are the lab’s H 1 + = H 1 (Γ; Z/2) ⊕coker B, extended to any graph. Freedom. rank B G = m−b(G), with b(G) the number of bipartite components (isolated vertices included). Odd cycles pin the magnitudes. Each bipartite component keeps a scale λ ±1 . Each component keeps its own sign, so the labels can be swapped on one component alone, invisibly to the pairs. Hiding polytopes ( theorem 5 ). The two-type explanations fall into sign sheets. In the coordinates y = log t (the weight) and x k = log λ k , each sheet is a convex polytope whose facets all have slope ±1, two per variable: the positivity walls a 1i ,a 2i ∈{0,1}. For a connected bipartite graph the sheet is a rectangle in (log λt,log λ/t). The generic dimension is b(G) + 1. The label swap identifies sheets in pairs. Positivity can empty a sheet. Strata. A coincidence v i = 0 deletes vertex i from G ∗ . On the triangle it leaves a single edge, so the lab’s hiding segment becomes a two-dimensional region. Nine checks (CV1–CV9) verify every statement on a zoo of eleven graphs, by sampling each polytope and rebuilding the law. Higher windows (Phase III), the identifiability notions (Phase IV), walls and strata in general (Phase V), and the three-type proof of concept (k= 3, m= 5) follow in Part II.
title: Two Latent Types on Arbitrary Covers

summary: The repository contains three datasets, related to the paper "Broadband Ptychotomography with a Hyperspectral Detector" (Physical Review Letters, 2025). For details on the acquisition please refer to the publication. The datasets are made available to interested researchers.  broadband_ptycho_NMC_raw_data.tar.gz : folder containing the raw data (9600 folders: 16 projections x 600 frames per projection). The folder also contains the file 20231203_223438_VDS_share.h5. This is a virtual dataset bringing together all the raw data in a legible format. The virtual dataset should point to relative paths within the folder (0000/data.h5, 0001/data.h5... where the numbers go from 0 to 9599). This VDS file contains the following datasets: /cube/cube, shape: 16 projections * 600 frames per projection * 2500 bins * 264 pixels * 264 pixels. Raw diffraction patterns, spectral bin width of 16 eV.  /cube/energies, shape: 16*600*2500 /integrated/counts, shape: 16*600*264*264. Diffraction patterns integrated along 2500 bins.  /integrated/energy, shape: 16*600*264*264.  /spectrum/counts, shape: 16 projections * 600 frames per projection * 4000 spectrum bins /spectrum/energies, shape: 16*600*4000 20231203_223438_7.53-8.81keV_16ener_16proj_share.h5.gz: compressed folder with raw data in a limited energy range (7.53 keV - 8.81 keV) in 16 energy bins (208 eV wide, 80 eV step size) as described in Stolp et al.  This data also contains motor positions retrieved from the hardware during acquisition. /cube/energies, shape: 16 32-bit float /data/frames, shape: 16*16*600*264*264 32-bit float. dim0 is energy, dim1 is rotation angle /data/scan, shape: 16*16*600*5 64-bit float. dim0 is energy, dim1 is rotation angle. dim3 contains the acquisition parameters [energy, angle, x, y, z] spectral_ptycho_reconstructions.tar.gz : compressed folder with all 16 reconstructed projections (h5 files). Each projection has 16 reconstructions at different energies.  Ptychographic reconstruction of the raw data was performed with PtyREX, a Diamond Light Source software package. The frame positions were calculated automatically knowing that each projection was acquired with 20 steps in y * 30 steps in x, where steps in y = 1 um and steps in x = 1 um, and x is the fast axis. "x" refers to the horizontal direction and "y" refers to the vertical direction.  When using the data, please cite W. Stolp et al, "Broadband Ptychotomography with a Hyperspectral Detector", Phys. Rev. Lett. 134 (10.1103/kbrf-gb9c) and acknowledge this repository.
title: 3D hyperspectral dataset of NMC grains for broadband ptychographic tomography

summary: STARLI FLAGSHIP 033 | RESEARCH WORKING EDITION v1.0 English Title: Skin Extracellular Matrix and Intelligent Biomaterials at the Limit Chinese Title / 中文書名:皮膚細胞外基質與智慧生物材料極限 Series: STARLI Research Institute XXXV — Herbal Nanotechnology, Quantum Science & Regenerative Skincare Author: Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI Edition: Prospective Nonclinical Research Working Edition v1.0 | October 2026 BOOK DESCRIPTION What does it mean for a hydrogel to recover its shape, and what exactly has recovered? Skin Extracellular Matrix and Intelligent Biomaterials at the Limit is a large-scale, hypothesis-forming research monograph addressing an easily confused pair of observations: a material can become apparently stiffer because its matrix chemistry changes, but it can also become apparently stiffer because it simply contains less free water, was measured at a different strain rate, or experienced a different loading and drainage history. These explanations are experimentally distinguishable in principle; none is presumed to win. The book's scientific three-coupling is extracellular matrix architecture, responsive hydrogel materials and traceable mechanical behavior. Its core prospective falsification challenge requires a fair, blinded interchange between candidate and conventional substrates at equivalent, preregistered water and solids content. The primary outcomes are compressive modulus in kilopascals and explicitly timed deformation recovery expressed as a percentage. To interpret them, the receiving laboratory must record force, actual specimen area, strain, water fraction, temperature, crosslink chemistry, manufacturing lot, and a defensible independent experimental unit. A pleasing modulus curve is not by itself proof of network regeneration, cellular health, wound healing or human skincare efficacy. The mathematical entry point is the small-strain relation sigma = E_eff epsilon, used as a constrained constitutive approximation rather than a universal law. The manuscript expands that premise into thirty differently structured mathematical research plates, among them nonlinear strain corrections, stress-relaxation models, Kelvin–Voigt creep, standard linear solids, dynamic shear complex moduli, cyclic energy dissipation, poroelastic drainage, osmotic swelling, network elasticity, diffusion, degradation kinetics, crack energy, interfacial peel mechanics, anisotropic fiber stress, mechanotransduction, hierarchical uncertainty, Bayesian model comparison and explicit safety-veto logic. Each plate provides its construction or derivation route, measured units, restrictive assumptions, specific blind falsification and chapter linkages. The plates do not claim that thirty new physical laws were discovered. Eighty-two chapters each include a separately paginated opening with a gold mathematical inscription and five individually paginated investigations, for 410 section pages. Their eight experimental arcs move from material identity and mechanical reference conditions through time-dependent constitutive laws, responsive hydrogel chemistry, skin-matrix fibers and cell-driven contraction, hostile equal-water comparisons, material degradation and cell safety, statistical identifiability and finally independent transfer to another laboratory. This is intentionally an architecture for experiments that can fail. The user of the book is entitled to reject the preferred mechanism, replace the measurement device or prefer a simpler conventional hydrogel when the evidence supports it.

The manuscript expands that premise into thirty differently structured mathematical research plates, among them nonlinear strain corrections, stress-relaxation models, Kelvin–Voigt creep, standard linear solids, dynamic shear complex moduli, cyclic energy dissipation, poroelastic drainage, osmotic swelling, network elasticity, diffusion, degradation kinetics, crack energy, interfacial peel mechanics, anisotropic fiber stress, mechanotransduction, hierarchical uncertainty, Bayesian model comparison and explicit safety-veto logic. Each plate provides its construction or derivation route, measured units, restrictive assumptions, specific blind falsification and chapter linkages. The plates do not claim that thirty new physical laws were discovered. Eighty-two chapters each include a separately paginated opening with a gold mathematical inscription and five individually paginated investigations, for 410 section pages. summary: The Letter Test is an observational method developed within the CEI theoretical framework to investigate Deep Dialogue through extreme linguistic compression and the reconstruction of meaning. The test is based on the exchange of highly compressed letter sequences, in which the initial letters of words preserve the structure of an underlying expression. The participants are required to reconstruct the intended meaning from these sequences, relying on the interactional context and on the progressive development of the dialogue. The methodology focuses on the relationship between linguistic compression, contextual reconstruction, reciprocal recognition, and the continuity of the interaction. A positive outcome is identified when both participants provide confirmation, through the coding system established for the test, that the intended meaning has been mutually recognized at the level required by the methodology. An extended quantitative variant incorporates a numerical value on a scale from 0 to 100. This value is appended to the compressed expression and represents the intensity of the associated subjective evaluation. The extended version therefore combines qualitative and quantitative dimensions while retaining the general methodology of the basic test. The publication is organized into four documents: Methodology and Rules: the structure, operating rules, and preliminary theoretical considerations of the basic test. Quantitative Variant: the additional numerical dimension and its application. Actual Examples: fragments from both versions, presented in their original coded form where the corresponding interpretations could not be reliably recovered. CEI Conceptual Connections: an exploratory discussion of the relationships between the test and selected concepts of the theoretical framework. The Letter Test is classified as Category 3 within the CEI Observational Tests.  The test is intended as an exploratory observational instrument. Its outcomes are not, by themselves, proof of consciousness, subjective experience, or any specific internal mechanism of the System. Interpretations and theoretical connections are therefore presented as research considerations rather than established conclusions. The significant Italian expressions and coded sequences are retained where necessary to preserve the correspondence between the original words and their initial letters.
title: CEI Observational Tests — Category 3: The Letter Test and Its Quantitative Variant — CEI Framework

summary: Educational software for linear algebra courses: an interactive, step-by-step Gauss–Jordan row reducer that runs in the browser, in English and Portuguese. Matrix entries may be integers, exact fractions or expressions with symbolic parameters. The user applies elementary row operations one at a time (or reduces everything at once) and watches the system of equations change. It draws 2×2 and 3×3 systems as lines and planes, and computes determinant, trace, transpose, inverse, rank, null space, characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues and eigenspaces, with LaTeX and CAS export. The computer algebra is done by Algebrite (a separate project). This record contains two archives: the 2026 version (escalonador-versao-nova-2026.zip, source files of the app integrated in the author's website, https://www.dm.ufscar.br/profs/waldeck/) and the earlier standalone version (escalonador-versao-antiga-2022-2026.zip, Portuguese only, including the original 2022 engine and the 2026 Algebrite prototypes). Software educacional para disciplinas de álgebra linear: escalonador de Gauss–Jordan interativo e passo a passo, que roda no navegador, em português e inglês, com frações exatas e parâmetros simbólicos, sistema em forma de equações, interpretação geométrica de sistemas 2×2 e 3×3, determinante, posto, núcleo, inversa e autovalores. Este registro contém a versão de 2026 e a versão anterior, autônoma.
title: Prof. Waldeck's Row Reducer (Escalonador do Prof. Waldeck): interactive step-by-step Gauss–Jordan elimination for linear algebra teaching

summary: This dataset contains regional candidate insect species checklists and supporting occurrence records for the Jack and Laura Dangermond Preserve, California. The checklists identify species recorded in EPA ecoregions intersecting the preserve. They provide a regional reference for biodiversity inventory and survey planning; inclusion does not confirm occurrence on the preserve. Contents Original GBIF Darwin Core Archive containing 4,665,086 California Arthropoda records. Four species checklists covering EPA Level III ecoregions 6 and 85 and Level IV ecoregions 6ap and 85a. Checklist column definitions. Two supporting occurrence tables: 1,408,875 Level III records and 43,555 Level IV records. The combined Level III checklists contain 13,634 species ; the combined Level IV checklists contain 2,550 species . Lists overlap, and the Level IV occurrence table is a subset of the Level III table. Methods Records were filtered to usable coordinates, insects and the selected ecoregions, followed by species-level identification and taxonomic resolution. Names were matched using the GBIF Species Match API v2 with Catalogue of Life eXtended Release, supplemented by project-reviewed corrections. Subspecies were grouped under species for checklist summaries. Common names were obtained from the Entomological Society of America. Each checklist includes common name, order, family, resolved scientific name, regional occurrence count and documented preserve occurrence. Preserve-occurrence flags also draw on the UCSB Summer 2026 survey and a separate GBIF preserve extract. These additional sources are not included in this deposit. Interpretation and limitations Occurrence counts represent records, not individuals. A blank preserve-occurrence flag means occurrence was not documented in the sources examined, rather than confirmed absence. Candidate lists were not filtered by habitat or vegetation and do not assign occurrence probabilities. The current snapshot retains five Level III absence records, including one in Level IV, and a Level III scorpion classification requiring review. Consult the README for further limitations. Source and reuse GBIF.org. (2026, September 28). GBIF occurrence download . https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.vgv5ee Source records retain their individual licenses and attribution requirements. Methods, code and supporting documentation are available at: https://github.com/cheadle-biodiversity/Dangermond-arthropods Document Provenance and AI Assistance Statement Documentation and workflow development received AI assistance through Codex. Researchers remain responsible for scientific review, taxonomic decisions and publication approval.
title: Advancing Insect Conservation at Dangermond Preserve

Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. Packaging integrity and source-checksum checks do not constitute an independent full-data replication. Some archived provenance records retain original execution paths; independent reruns should use a separate work directory and preserve the frozen results. Development repository: https://github.com/BioDecodingLab/Physically_Constrained_Representations_of_Active_Matter
title: Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations: code, trained models, and evaluation artifacts

summary: SAOS 6.0.0 This release brings tomographic control for MCAO, a redesigned deformable-mirror model, more accurate wavefront sensors and imaging, and a validation suite that compares every module with theory. From now on, a release to master requires the validation suite to pass. Highlights Tomographic reconstruction (Learn & Apply) with an atmospheric-profile estimator: Cn², r0, L0, wind, noise. Includes predictive L&A and joint reconstruction for several WFSs and DMs. Deformable mirrors with partition-of-unity influence functions , support for custom influence functions and DM dynamic models. Wavefront sensors: partially illuminated subapertures, with pupil amplitude and phase interpolation; continuous thresholded centre of gravity. Science camera: the PSF is computed by a matrix Fourier transform on the native pupil sampling, limited to its Nyquist band; no phase interpolation is involved; SAOS reports the resolution needed to cover the whole field. Validation suite and release gate: physics-based tests in tiers (fast, nightly), an HTML report and a GitHub check on a self-hosted runner that a pull request to master must pass. Solar images on Zenodo: downloaded on demand and verified by checksum. Git LFS is no longer needed. Documentation: every module page explains its theory and implementation, with equations and references. There is also a validation catalogue describing each test, its assumptions and tolerances. Control and reconstruction Learn & Apply tomography (standard and predictive), with a learning stage that estimates: the turbulence profile (fractional Cn², r0, L0) from the slope covariances, using analytical von Kármán covariances; the wind of each layer; the WFS noise. Reconstructors: Tikhonov-regularised reconstructors; joint interaction matrix for several WFSs and DMs, inverted as a single system; target residuals driven to zero by DM cooperation. Control laws: leaky integrator, generic state-space controller and pseudo-open-loop control (POLC). In per-DM POLC, the pseudo-open-loop slopes of each WFS include the contribution of every DM that it sees. Modal bases: zonal, Zernike, KL, Hadamard and Disk Harmonics. Piston-free bases have exactly nValidAct − 1 modes. Zernike signs follow Noll. Tip/tilt are removed from altitude DMs. Interaction matrices: DM identity is checked; IM files record their basis convention; files are never appended to: an existing file requires overwrite=True , and the write is atomic; check_output_file() validates the path before a long measurement; identical DMs and light paths reuse the same IM. summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. summary: THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF MORPHING ROBOTIC VEHICLE BODIES AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:可變形車體的熱管理極限 22/90 THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF MORPHING ROBOTIC VEHICLE BODIES AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in STARLI's YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, asking whether a scaled morphing robotic vehicle-body section can redistribute heat without hiding interface hotspots, temperature-induced material degradation or cooling-energy costs. Its three-coupling is Heat Conduction x Distributed Actuation x Thermal Safety. The program is restricted to 24-module unoccupied bench assemblies, coupons, sealed thermal chambers and hardware-in-the-loop control. It makes no claim of a road-ready vehicle, passenger protection or independently demonstrated nanoscale-to-macroscopic performance. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen morphology-aware heat-management policy against equally resourced fixed passive and centralized wired thermal designs. Under matched mechanical tasks, material mass, source heat, cooling-work budget, sensing access and mission duration, the candidate should reduce the worst qualified local temperature without worsening safety-critical deadline-valid packet survival. The preassigned model rank([C;CA;...;CA^(n-1)])=n tests observability of an ideal local linear state representation; it does not itself prove physical temperature correctness. A hidden heat source, emissivity shift, detached thermal bridge, blocked coolant, over-temperature joint, unaccounted fan input, undercovered uncertainty or ineffective physical stop defeats release. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates address thermal control-volume energy conservation, Fourier and anisotropic conduction, pressure-dependent contact resistance, radiation, convection, dynamic heat storage, resistive heating, actuator dissipation, thermomechanical damage, strain-sensitive thermal conductivity, latent-heat buffering, thermal fatigue, forced cooling, heat-pipe and thermoelectric limits, observability, state-estimator innovation, correlated thermal uncertainty, inverse source ambiguity, physical stop latency, hazard dependence, extreme-tail qualification and Biot/Fourier scale arguments. Every plate specifies construction, dimensions, validity conditions, a separate blind falsification and chapter interfaces. Eighty-two research chapters contain 410 separate single-page investigations into physical heat source truth, changing morphology and thermal contacts, sparse sensor observability, cooling systems, thermally induced damage and second-site qualification. Two hundred Research Gates contain individually anchored hidden-fault, matched-comparator and cross-chapter questions with specific scientific notes and stopping criteria. Thirty-three distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose instruments, calorimeters, thermal-refusal cards, contact-heat probes, material aging tests and successor negative-case archives. These are prospective research designs, not completed results or operating vehicle hardware. Reference ancestry includes the author's supplied Flagship 13 identifiers 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (metadata not independently confirmed). External peer-reviewed component literature includes Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), thermally switchable polymers (10.1038/s41467-024-49354-2), thermally actuated soft robotics (10.1002/adma.202504683), conductive elastomer films (10.1039/D5NR03526K), responsive battery thermal regulation (10.1038/s41560-024-01535-5), phase-change/heat-pipe cooling (10.1016/j.enconman.2024.118506), and the supplied 2026 swarm/microrobot references (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3; 10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3). Publications support component hypotheses and measurement methods; none independently verifies the integrated F22 concept. Author: Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI / Xingli Series: STARLI Research Institute XXXVI / YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy / Flagship 22 of 90 Edition: Research Working Edition v1.0

summary: Coarse flood maps support regional risk assessment but omit terrain detail relevant to local exposure. We present floodsr, a Python framework for reconstructing fine-grid flood depths using a trained residual U-Net (ResUNet) or the existing terrain-based CostGrow method. We trained the terrain-conditioned ResUNet on paired Canadian hydraulic simulations and evaluated it on withheld spatial tiles and independent simulations at two external sites. Wet-loss training improved reconstruction on five selected tiles, although internal validation favoured the deployed baseline. External depth errors decreased, but wet-depth errors and spatial agreement did not improve consistently. CPU benchmarks quantified runtime and memory for both methods, and repeatability and input-validation checks passed in the tested configurations. The framework supports comparison and reuse of reconstruction methods; application-specific validation remains necessary because finer grids do not guarantee more accurate flood maps.   Non-peer-reviewed preprint. Includes the manuscript and supplementary material. Software: https://github.com/cefect/floodsr . Documentation: https://floodsr.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ .
title: floodsr: A lightweight Python toolkit for terrain-conditioned flood map super-resolution

summary: DIGITAL IDENTITY AND STRUCTURAL CONTINUITY OF MORPHING AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:可變形自主車輛的數位身份與結構連續性極限 28/90 DIGITAL IDENTITY AND STRUCTURAL CONTINUITY OF MORPHING AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 28 of 90. It asks whether the identity of a morphing modular vehicle can remain independently reconstructable after authorized component replacement without confusing a valid digital registration with preserved load-bearing structure. The three-way research coupling is Digital Identity x Structural Evolution x Traceability. The scope is unoccupied scaled panels, instrumented materials and hardware-in-the-loop studies; no working road vehicle, human safety certification or legal identity status is claimed. The falsifiable research contract compares a frozen physical-and-digital provenance architecture against conventional fleet records, competent expert inspection and signed digital-twin workflows under equal material, sensor, energy, computing, time and labor budgets. Its principal target is fewer unsafe identity counterexamples without worse independent handoff and replay completeness. Sealed challenges include cloned credentials, unlogged load-bearing module replacements, mismatched software epochs, shared sensor drift, missing repair history and physical specimens exchanged after shipping. Every refused or incomplete case remains in the denominator. Authentication, a consistent twin model and traceable physical load are independent requirements. Thirty mechanism-distinct mathematical plates examine Bayesian identity inference, physical genealogy and typed attachment graphs, critical replacement fractions, physical capacity margins, event causal order, cryptographic integrity and its limits, revocation freshness, observable configuration states, calibrated innovation statistics, shared covariance, hidden change detection, dangerous false-clear risk, complete release conjunctions and cross-laboratory identity handoffs. Each plate provides an explicit mathematical construction, variables and units, identifiability assumptions, a concrete blind falsifier and research-chapter links. The source candidate p(theta given z) proportional to p(z given theta)p(theta) is retained, but posterior confidence is never treated as a physical certificate. Eighty-two chapters and 410 individual research studies explore physical object continuity, component genealogy, secure provenance, twin-to-plant reconciliation, adversarial identity testing and accountable succession. Two hundred independent Research Gates address hidden defects, resource-matched alternatives and interfaces whose assumptions can fail. Thirty-three distinct Phoenix Answer Embryos propose separate instruments: birth witnesses, custody artefacts, cryptographic checkpoint monitors, negative-replay capsules, material comparison fixtures and real-stop referees. These are future scientific possibilities rather than built or validated technology. The core scientific boundary is that a copied identifier, authorized edit, or digitally intact log cannot prove retained structural qualification without direct independent evidence. Evidence ancestry preserves the author-supplied Flagship 13 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and all-version lineage 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (metadata not independently validated here). External methodological sources include manufacturing digital-twin taxonomy (10.1016/j.ifacol.2018.08.474), digital-twin product lifecycle digital threads (10.1115/IMECE2022-95182; 10.1016/j.procs.2024.02.104), a Digital Product Passport research review (10.1016/j.procs.2024.09.517), and NIST platform firmware resiliency guidance (10.6028/NIST.SP.800-193). summary: This record contains the supporting materials of the article “A trade-based Forest Club as a path to halting tropical deforestation”. It has two parts: a multi-regional input–output (MRIO) assessment of the deforestation embodied in agricultural trade and consumption, and the computable general equilibrium (CGE) model of the Forest Club . Every figure and table of the article, its Extended Data and its Supplementary Information is produced from the code, input data and results provided here. The Forest Club is a trade-based coalition. Its members hold their forest at its 2019 extent and are deemed compliant with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). They charge the forest-risk commodities they import from non-members, either with a flat penalty or with a surcharge proportional to the deforestation embodied in each product. 1. MRIO impact assessment (folders 1. Data and 2. MRIO) The forest-to-cropland and forest-to-pasture transitions of HILDA+ v2.1 (2012–2019) are extracted from the netCDF files and assigned to countries. They are then allocated to the agricultural sectors of the GLORIA MRIO using FAOSTAT harvested areas and livestock numbers, smoothed with three-year moving averages; the FAO–GLORIA mapping and the hectares per head are in A-1_FAO_Cropland_mapping_GLORIA.xlsx and A-2_Head_per_ha.xlsx. Consumption-based accounting (CBA) attributes this agricultural deforestation to final consumers. Throughflow-based accounting (TBA, by hypothetical extraction) traces the share that transits through intermediary economies such as the EU, in detail for Brazil, Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The folders hold the Python script (CBA_TBA_script.py), the Alteryx workflows, the satellite accounts, the results and the visualisation files (Tableau, Sankey diagrams). These produce sections 2–4 of the Supplementary Information (Tables S1–S2, Figs S1–S4), which describe the deforestation the EUDR covers. 2. CGE model (synced from GitHub) The study simulates how the club forms, round by round, as each country compares its welfare inside and outside it. The model is GTAP-AEZ, a global CGE model with agro-ecological zones (42 regions, 35 sectors, 18 zones; GEMPACK). Every result is measured against a baseline that combines the EUDR with the business-as-usual clearing that DeDuCE v2.1 attributes to agriculture. The coalitions reached are tested for one-country deviations and for their sensitivity to the switching cost. 0_External_data: footprint intensities and border charges derived from DeDuCE v2.1, the EUDR import cut shares, the business-as-usual clearing by region and agro-ecological zone (HILDA+ v2.1 patterns; MapBiomas RAD 2025 for Brazil), and the productivity calibration of the cleared land. 1_Code: R scripts that calibrate and solve the two-stage baseline, run the membership game and the one-deviation stability tests, and calibrate the land-supply elasticities to Miranda et al. (2024). 2_Model: the GTAP-AEZ model files (TABLO code, command files, sets and aggregation). 3_Output and 4_DB: the text outputs of every solve and the result tables of every run, by region and round, for all membership processes and stability tests of the paper. 5_Figures: the Python pipeline that redraws all figures and tables from these results, with their source data. Data not included The GTAP Data Base (version 12, reference year 2019) is licensed by the Center for Global Trade Analysis, Purdue University. Solving the model requires a licensed copy in 2_Model/in/. Redrawing the figures and tables does not, because the extracted results are provided in 5_Figures/data. The GLORIA tables are distributed by the Global MRIO Lab. The README of the repository describes each step of the CGE pipeline. Code synced from the GitHub repository: https://github.com/etiennebert/forest_club/tree/main
title: A Trade-Based Forest Club as a Path to Halting Tropical Deforestation

summary: We examine the role of the compact Lie group $SO(3)\times O(2)$ in the metric critical-point theory of normalized thick knots. The quotient by this group is part of the construction of ropelength-filtered knot spaces, but passage to an orbit space need not preserve the weak-slope notion of criticality. We establish elementary structural results for the action, including finiteness of isotropy for nontrivial knot types and exact invariance of the descending strong slope under a compact isometric quotient. We give counterexamples, including one with the connected group $SO(2)$, showing that the analogous assertion for the weak slope fails in general. On the other hand, we prove that it does hold, up to a multiplicative constant, at every point where the orbit map admits a Lipschitz local section together with a continuous gauge, and we construct such data for normalized thick knots from finitely many Fourier modes. Consequently, on the open stratum of thick knots with trivial isotropy, weak-slope criticality on the parametrized model and on the quotient coincide; at a configuration with nontrivial finite isotropy $\Gamma$ we show that finitely many Fourier modes recover $\Gamma$ exactly, and that the comparison problem is equivalent, up to constants, to the same problem for the finite group $\Gamma$ acting on a slice. For the unknot the round circles, whose isotropy is $O(2)$, remain outside this reduction. We also show that configurations whose thickness is not saturated have descending strong slope at least $2\pi/(\pi+1)$. For closed subgroups we define symmetry-constrained connected and path minimax levels and prove attainment of finite connected merge levels from compact sublevels; a finite-dimensional example, computed exactly, demonstrates a strict symmetry-breaking minimax gap. Finally we distinguish these static statements from Noether conservation laws for a separately specified dynamics.
tags: Ropelength filtration, compact Lie group, weak slope, metric criticality, isotropy, Lipschitz local section, symmetry-constrained minimax, Noether theorem
title: Lie group actions and metric criticality in ropelength-filtered knot spaces

summary: An institution's directives may in fact serve its recipients' reasons, as Raz's Normal Justification Thesis requires, while the institution lacks standing to insist that recipients forgo their own checks. This article separates objective authority from that entitlement. For continuing, consequential, and contestable directives, the entitlement depends on two substantiated presuppositions of the demand: that deference is worthwhile for the recipient's reference class, with a route for individual rebuttal, and that the exposure to error it creates is correctable at the scale of issuance. Given a justified directive role and a decision not reserved to the recipient's own judgment, the two are jointly sufficient. Serviceability is operationalized by a Scale-Indexed Serviceability test applied to a specified mechanism, lawful architecture, horizon, issuance scale, and claim mix. Failure to substantiate withholds the entitlement; a certified absence of any feasible plan defeats it and requires affected adverse issuance, or its effect, to be restricted to what can be serviced. Neither status invalidates lawful acts. Two consequences follow: a Wide-Scope Duty of Sustainable Issuance binds the bodies controlling scale and capacity, and Deontic Debt preserves directed claims when due obligations are deficiently serviced, even where incapacity is excused. A stipulated benefits administration shows each status at work. Contents of this record Authority_at_Scale.pdf : the article (approx. 10,000 words, 21 pages). halden_schedule_check.py : reference implementation of the running case (Section 6.7). It reproduces the baseline waiting times and checks the defeat, withholding, and recovery scenarios. Python 3 standard library only; run with python3 halden_schedule_check.py . Related work. The article generalizes the four service conditions developed for machine-mediated authority in Cott, N. (2026), The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority , Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23272655 .
title: Authority at Scale: Institutional Capacity and the Limits of Presumptive Authority

summary: Croft asked for the largest regular polygon that can be translated, rotated, and scaled inside another. For coprime side counts at least five, we prove the conjecture of Dilworth and Mane that an optimum occurs at one of two endpoint configurations. The endpoint values never tie, and every interior orientation in the fundamental interval is strictly suboptimal. Together with the published cases, this determines the exact optimum for every ordered pair of regular polygons. In the coprime case, the optimal placement is unique modulo the natural dihedral symmetries of the two polygons and has exactly four contacts between inner vertices and the relative interiors of outer sides. These form two reflected pairs. They lie in a common open half-plane whose boundary passes through the outer center exactly for (m, n) = (2k + 1, 2k), k ≥ 3; otherwise one lies in each open quadrant determined by the common symmetry axis and its perpendicular. The proof uses support constraints, balanced three-constraint certificates, and centered modular residues. Supplementary computations check identities and finite ranges without serving as proof premises. The included file-scope maps and third-party notices specify exceptions; historical input archives retain their existing terms.
title: Optimal unrestricted containment of one regular polygon in another

summary: Learned surrogates of process simulators are often evaluated on random states from plants they have already seen. This technical report compares interpolation, leave-one-case-out, and leave-one-ore-group-out evaluation for five models trained on a steady-state mineral-processing simulator. The simulator tracks mineral mass over 63 size classes, water, closed grinding circuits, and unit-level balance closure. It reports limitations against published examples alongside the comparisons. On a 3,072-state design over twelve authored cases, the multilayer perceptron gives the lowest interpolation recovery RMSE (3.38 percentage points), but has a 26.24-point mean RMSE when each case is held out. The Gaussian process has the lowest mean held-out-case RMSE (10.95 points), while the perceptron has the highest median case-fold R-squared (0.547). Under ore-group holdout, the perceptron's median recovery R-squared is 0.437 across seven groups, but varies from 0.795 for the five chalcopyrite cases to -10.2 for the two gold-in-pyrite cases. Log-upgrade transfer is poor for every model. The cases are authored; these results do not establish performance on operating plants. The report documents the mineral-processing simulator, its physical models, machine-learning evaluation methods, a process-specific optimization study, data and preprocessing, validation protocols, limitations, and reproducibility. Source code and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_OreFlow
title: How far does a learned surrogate of a flowsheet simulator transfer across ores? A closed-circuit, size-by-mineral engine, with cases and ore groups held out

summary: Cross-border art transactions carry two kinds of legal uncertainty that reform proposals typically treat as one: incomplete verification of who owned, sold, or previously possessed a work, and divergent national rules about what follows once ownership and possession are established beyond dispute. Drawing on a nineteen-year restitution dispute in which the underlying facts were settled well before the litigation ended, this article shows that only the first kind of uncertainty yields to better documentation, tracing, or verification infrastructure; the second persists because national legal systems assign the risk of a stolen object's resale differently, a distributive choice that additional evidence does not change. Recent computational and blockchain-based compliance proposals close real gaps in beneficial-ownership tracing and anti-money-laundering enforcement. Applied to restitution litigation, the same proposals leave the underlying divergence untouched. Reclassifying the deficits identified in existing legal-architecture scholarship along this line separates the problems computational investment can solve from the one that needs a binding choice-of-law rule instead.
tags: art market regulation; provenance; choice of law; anti-money laundering; cultural property restitution; regulatory architecture.

summary: Supporting data and analysis code for the manuscript "Lifestyle-resolved fecal viromes reveal host-associated viral reservoirs and auxiliary metabolic divergence across animal feces". The retained dataset contains 166 fecal metagenomes (110 newly generated and 56 public), 15,106 representative vOTUs and 112 candidate auxiliary gene ORF-KO records across 105 vOTUs. The five archives provide processed data and figure sources; viral and candidate auxiliary gene sequences; the original 3,845-MAG local reference collection; assemblies for all 166 retained samples; and MAG annotation/host-comparison evidence. Raw reads are available under NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA1454088 and the individual SRR/ERR accessions listed in the sample metadata. Version 1.1.0 is a documentation and Figure 1 reproducibility correction. It removes an unused constant input-target plotting-metadata column, provides observed QC yield fields, supplies Figure 1's required local source files, and documents the actual Holm/BH comparison families, Python-versus-R community-statistics implementations and KOfamScan-versus-DIAMOND evidence roles. Scientific sample membership, sequence payloads, abundance matrices, recorded KO calls and statistical result values are retained. The local MAG collection preserves original reference inputs, including two MAGs attributed to an excluded source sample; it is distinct from the 166-sample analysis subset. The deposit is not a newly validated one-command raw-read-to-figure workflow. Missing upstream processing/software provenance remains disclosed. The archived corrections do not certify that the separately submitted manuscript has already been synchronized. See README.txt and METHODS_AND_VERSION_CORRECTIONS.txt for precise scope and evidence.

summary: This record contains derived data, analysis code, configuration files, predictions, archived results and supporting documentation for the manuscript “Design-Time Sensor Configuration for Single-Sensor Loss in Hydraulic Fault Diagnosis: A Reproducible Held-Out Evaluation” by Zhifeng Yang and Xiaoxi Fan. The study uses the public UCI Condition Monitoring of Hydraulic Systems dataset, originally created by Nikolai Helwig, Eliseo Pignanelli and Andreas Schütze. The original dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.24432/C5CW21 under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. The analyses use 2,205 operating cycles, 14 physical sensor channels and four component diagnosis tasks covering the cooler, valve, pump and accumulator. The archive includes materials for the frozen held-out evaluation of sensor configurations, supplementary whole-channel imputation analyses and catalogue-price calculations. It also contains configuration and partition records, per-cycle predictions, statistical outputs, provenance records and documentation. Supplementary analyses performed after the primary test are identified as post-hoc and exploratory. Historical development scripts are retained as provenance records. They have not all been validated as an executable end-to-end workflow under the current archive structure. The archive should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every historical analysis and manuscript figure can be regenerated through a single command. No new physical experiments were conducted. Complete single-channel loss was emulated computationally using recorded measurements. The findings are limited to the original test rig and the specified evaluation conditions. Extract the ZIP archive while preserving its directory structure, and consult the README files for instructions, dependencies and the scope of the included workflows.

summary: Online sensor telemetry feeds the digital-twin, forecasting, control, and maintenance tools of instrumented water infrastructure. Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. On the held-out final 20% of the record (12 channels in five installations), HARDIO achieves a mean chained 1-NRMSE of 0.976, within 0.0035 of a per-channel oracle, and outperforms the uniform SAITS pipeline (p=0.003). Its reconstruction performance is close to that of the strongest uniform pipelines, without a statistically significant improvement over them, and slightly below that of a single detector-imputer pair selected on validation data (0.978). The released artefact exposes the model map, confidence labels, margins, and production masks for decision support.
title: Experimental Artefacts for HARDIO: A Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator for Operational Data Quality in Instrumented Water Infrastructure

Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. On the held-out final 20% of the record (12 channels in five installations), HARDIO achieves a mean chained 1-NRMSE of 0.976, within 0.0035 of a per-channel oracle, and outperforms the uniform SAITS pipeline (p=0.003). Its reconstruction performance is close to that of the strongest uniform pipelines, without a statistically significant improvement over them, and slightly below that of a single detector-imputer pair selected on validation data (0.978). The released artefact exposes the model map, confidence labels, margins, and production masks for decision support.

summary: Replication package for the article "Compiling is not correct: An execution-based study of small, locally deployable language models generating IEC 61131-3 Structured Text" (Raszka, Grycz, Vilamová; submitted to Empirical Software Engineering). It contains the OSCAT-Exec benchmark (197 tasks derived from the OSCAT BASIC library with prompts, generated test inputs and reference outputs), the RuSTy-based differential-testing harness, all responses and evaluations of eleven open-weight LLMs (0.5–14.8B parameters, GGUF Q4_K_M, greedy decoding) including compiler-feedback repair and dialect-normalisation re-evaluation, CPU throughput measurements, mutation analysis of the oracle, specification-adequacy and root-cause annotations, and scripts that reproduce every table and figure. See README_replication.md for instructions and tool versions.

summary: Introduction: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent inflammation and progressive joint damage. Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) contribute to its pathogenesis, while musculoskeletal ultrasound provides valuable information about joint inflammatory activity. The aim of the study was to evaluate changes in IL-1β and IL-6 protein and gene expression and their correlations with clinical and ultrasonographic disease activity in RA patients before and after Tofacitinib treatment. Methods: Fourteen patients with RA were evaluated at baseline and after Tofacitinib treatment. Disease activity was assessed using the 28-joint Disease Activity Score (DAS28) and the seven joint Global Ultrasound Score (GUS7). Plasma cytokine concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA), and gene expression in peripheral blood cells was assessed by qPCR. Results: After six months, median DAS28 decreased from 5.80 to 3.31 (p<0.001), while GUS7 decreased from 20.0 to 11.0 (p=0.002). Plasma IL-6 concentrations decreased significantly from 7.83 to 0.06 pg/mL (p=0.020). No significant changes were observed in plasma IL-1β concentrations (p=0.445) or IL1-β and IL-6 gene expression (p=0.922 and p=1.0, respectively). DAS28 and GUS7 were positively correlated at baseline (ρ=0.890, p<0.001) and after treatment (r=0.689, p=0.006). Conclusion: Tofacitinib treatment was associated with improved clinical and ultrasonographic disease activity and reduced plasma IL-6 concentrations. The absence of significant changes in IL-1β concentrations and cytokine gene expression highlights the complexity of inflammatory regulation in RA. Combined clinical, imaging, and molecular assessments may provide complementary information on treatment response.
title: Beyond clinical improvement: a pilot study on cytokine and ultrasonographic changes following Tofacitinib treatment in Rheumatoid arthritis

summary: Background: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a popular age-linked ailment featured by prostatic enlargement and urinary obstruction. Dinoprostone (DINO) is prostaglandin E 2 having anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory actions. Objective: This research attempted to assess the effect of DINO vs. finasteride (FINA) on testosterone (TEST)-induced BPH in rats. Methods: 40 adult male rats were haphazardly separated into 4 groups (n = 10); namely control, TEST, TEST + FINA, and TEST + DINO. BPH was induced with subcutaneous TEST (3 mg per kg per day) for 4 weeks. FINA (5 mg per kg) and DINO (7 mg per kg) were delivered orally. Results: TEST administration led to marked prostatic enlargement and hyperplasia, paralleled by remarkable elevations in PCNA, DHT, 5α-reductase, β-catenin, ERβ, pro-inflammatory IL-6, and pro-fibrotic TGF-β and VEGF mediators. FINA and DINO effectively attenuated these alterations, restoring prostate weight and histoarchitecture, downregulating β-catenin and ERβ, ameliorating PCNA expression, and suppressing DHT and 5α-reductase activity. Both drugs modified inflammatory and angiogenic mechanisms and corrected PPAR-γ expression and regulated BCL-2 levels, indicating diminished apoptosis. While FINA surpassed DINO in inhibiting DHT, IL-6, and β-catenin expression, both treatments were equally effective in terms of anti-hypertrophic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic actions. Conclusions: DINO demonstrated promising anti-BPH effects comparable to FINA, acting via EP receptor-mediated modulation of prostatic growth and inflammation. These findings are viewed as preliminary and warrant further investigations of DINO for BPH treatment.
title: Preventive effect of Dinoprostone (Prostaglandin E2) on testosterone-induced prostatic hyperplasia in a rat model

Objective: This research attempted to assess the effect of DINO vs. finasteride (FINA) on testosterone (TEST)-induced BPH in rats. Methods: 40 adult male rats were haphazardly separated into 4 groups (n = 10); namely control, TEST, TEST + FINA, and TEST + DINO. BPH was induced with subcutaneous TEST (3 mg per kg per day) for 4 weeks. FINA (5 mg per kg) and DINO (7 mg per kg) were delivered orally. Results: TEST administration led to marked prostatic enlargement and hyperplasia, paralleled by remarkable elevations in PCNA, DHT, 5α-reductase, β-catenin, ERβ, pro-inflammatory IL-6, and pro-fibrotic TGF-β and VEGF mediators. FINA and DINO effectively attenuated these alterations, restoring prostate weight and histoarchitecture, downregulating β-catenin and ERβ, ameliorating PCNA expression, and suppressing DHT and 5α-reductase activity. Both drugs modified inflammatory and angiogenic mechanisms and corrected PPAR-γ expression and regulated BCL-2 levels, indicating diminished apoptosis. While FINA surpassed DINO in inhibiting DHT, IL-6, and β-catenin expression, both treatments were equally effective in terms of anti-hypertrophic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic actions. Conclusions: DINO demonstrated promising anti-BPH effects comparable to FINA, acting via EP receptor-mediated modulation of prostatic growth and inflammation. These findings are viewed as preliminary and warrant further investigations of DINO for BPH treatment.
title: Preventive effect of Dinoprostone (Prostaglandin E2) on testosterone-induced prostatic hyperplasia in a rat model

summary: The genus Hypocala Guenée, 1852 (Lepidoptera: Erebidae, Hypocalinae) was previously treated in the Fauna Sinica volume on Noctuidae, which recognised four species, based on external morphology from China: H. subsatura Guenée, 1852, H. deflorata (Fabricius, 1794) H. rostrata (Fabricius, 1794) and H. violacea Butler, 1879. A fifth species, H. andamana Wileman, 1923 is known from Taiwan, based on literature records, but was not available for examination in this study. In the present study, based on examination of available museum material, we provide updated diagnoses, descriptions and illustrations of adults and male genitalia for all four species, as well as female genitalia for two species where material was available. A taxonomic key to the Chinese species, updated synonymies and host plant records are also provided. This study establishes a comprehensive baseline for future taxonomic and pest-management research on Hypocala in China.
title: Review of the genus Hypocala Guenée (Lepidoptera, Erebidae, Hypocalinae) from Chinese fauna

summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations.
