Full concurrent deployment produces the constitutional infrastructure specifically suited to the failure mode the existing literature identifies but has not prescribed for: authoritarian federal capture by actors engaged in the systematic dismantling of democratic governance and the rule of law. The doctrinal foundation draws on dual sovereignty, the anti-commandeering doctrine, intergovernmental immunity, and the Tenth Amendment's structural reservation of sovereign authority to the states, doctrines consistently applied across two and a half centuries of American constitutional law because they reflect the Constitution's design rather than any particular political moment. Notably, the anti-commandeering doctrine at the architecture's foundation was built by conservative jurisprudence for entirely different purposes. Justice Scalia wrote Printz to protect states from federal gun control mandates. The doctrine he articulated does not ask which political faction is deploying it. They enable every tier of this framework, from refusing federal cooperation to prosecuting federal officials, without federal permission, federal oversight, or presidential interference. The framework does not conflict with the Supremacy Clause, which governs conflicts between state and federal regulatory regimes and has never been understood to immunize federal officials from state criminal liability for conduct that violates state law, to compel states to assist federal enforcement, or to displace the paralle
title: THE CONSTITUTIONAL ARCHITECTURE OF STATE OPPOSITION

summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?

summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

summary: Optimizing discrete allocation weights across competing segments of a shared budget is a fundamental challenge in resource-constrained, sequential decision-making environments. In practice, this optimization is often hindered by delayed, noisy, and aggregate feedback, alongside strict operational constraints on how frequently weights can be adjusted. Because of the resulting combinatorial action space and extreme data sparsity, classical multi-armed bandit algorithms that evaluate arms independently are rendered highly inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we propose a segmentation-agnostic approach utilizing Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (GP-UCB) algorithms. By placing a Gaussian Process prior on the reward function, our method effectively shares information across neighboring configurations, drastically reducing the necessary exploration horizon. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theoretical bandit research and production-scale deployment. We first introduce a high-fidelity synthetic simulator to evaluate various kernel configurations under stationary, drifting, and reactive environments, identifying a composite Matérn + Linear kernel as the most robust choice for overcoming local noise and global shifts. Finally, we validate our findings through a large-scale Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) in a live production environment. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GP-UCB approach delivers a statistically significant efficiency lift compared to a standard $\varepsilon$-greedy baseline, offering a highly practical solution for real-world black-box lever optimization.
title: Gaussian Process Bandits for Constraint Black Box Lever Optimization

summary: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding

summary: This work investigates how site-specific digital twins (DTs) can support wireless localization using simplified distributed infrastructure. We propose PRISM (Probabilistic Refinement using Inverse learning and a Site-specific Model), a DT-guided probabilistic localization scheme with single-antenna access points (APs). Localization is formulated as a probabilistic inverse problem in which a conditional proposal distribution over UE locations is learned from multi-node channel impulse responses (CIRs). The proposal generates candidate locations, with its spread regularized during training and DT consistency used to reweight candidates and refine the estimate at inference. The DT serves as an approximate forward-consistency model, avoiding assumptions of exact channel fidelity or differentiability with respect to user position. Numerical experiments demonstrate gains over data-driven and classical fingerprinting benchmarks, while achieving a median error of approximately $0.7$ m using 10 single-antenna APs. Without retraining, PRISM remains effective under degraded inference-time DT features. PRISM also yields uncertainty estimates from its proposal covariance, with empirical $χ^2$ calibration approaching ideal behavior as APs increase.
title: Digital Twin-Guided Wireless Localization via Probabilistic Inverse Learning

summary: Gradient-based data attribution has become an important tool for high-quality data selection in the instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), as it estimates the contribution of training examples through their influence on model optimization. However, we find that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from surface-form bias: minor changes to semantically irrelevant details, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content remains unchanged. To address this issue, we propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA), a robust framework for instruction data selection. CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, thereby reducing formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. CIGA also reduces attribution cost, offering a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.
title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution

summary: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation

summary: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression

summary: Modeling multi-scale dynamics in urban road networks is essential for intelligent transportation systems but is often hindered by the computational cost of long-range historical context and the challenge of fusing heterogeneous modalities. Existing spatio-temporal frameworks face a trade-off between sequence length and memory overhead, while frequently neglecting the transient effects of exogenous factors such as road incidents and weather. To address these limitations, we propose SpecLST, a frequency-enhanced long-short-term spatio-temporal multimodal framework. SpecLST leverages a fast Fourier transform-based frequency-domain representation module to efficiently encode multi-week historical dependencies, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of standard attention mechanisms over raw long sequences. Heterogeneous context is integrated through attention-based fusion, followed by a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation for spatio-temporal representation learning. Additionally, a frequency-enhanced residual head isolates high-frequency transients, improving sensitivity to abrupt traffic anomalies. At the 60-minute horizon, SpecLST achieves mean relative error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across eight neural forecasting baselines and four datasets, with the dataset- and metric-specific average reductions ranging from 5.63% to 22.21%.
title: SpecLST: Spectral-Enhanced Long-Short Term Spatio-Temporal Multimodal Modeling for Traffic Forecasting

summary: This paper is concerned with the simultaneous recovery of the trajectory and intensity of an unknown moving point source in an inhomogeneous acoustic medium. We prove that the whole-boundary measurements over a finite time interval uniquely determine the moving source. Furthermore, under suitable propagation and rank assumptions, Lipschitz stability of determining both the trajectory and intensity is derived using waveforms measured at four fixed receivers outside the source region. A novel Volterra--Euler reconstruction scheme is developed for solving the inverse problem, and the error estimate is derived for the proposed scheme. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed numerical method.
title: An inverse moving point source problem in inhomogeneous acoustic media: uniqueness, stability and reconstruction

summary: We have discovered an inverse relationship between the earthquake source deactivation coefficient and the magnitude of the main shock. Recently, this pattern was confirmed through an analysis of earthquakes in the Central Himalayas (Poudel et al., 2026). On the one hand, independent confirmation of a previously unknown pattern strengthens our confidence in the relevance of the phenomenological theory of aftershocks, upon which we have based our method for processing and analyzing aftershocks. On the other hand, Poudel et al. (2026) presented our method in a distorted manner. Poudel et al. mistakenly believe that our method is based on a modified Omori law. Both circumstances provide an occasion and a basis for a simple and clear explanation of the essence of our approach to the study of aftershocks. First and foremost, our approach to the problem is diametrically opposed to Omori approach. Omori law and its modification, proposed by Hirano and Utsu, describe the decay of aftershocks. In contrast, we formulated and solved the inverse problem. The essence of the inverse problem lies in the need to calculate the source deactivation coefficient based on aftershock observation data, without making any prior assumptions regarding the law governing the decay of aftershocks. A crucial concept in our theory is the rather complex notion of the proper time of a source. Proper time differs radically from astronomical time. The paper describes the continuous and discrete representations of proper time. This paper is methodological in nature and may prove useful to researchers studying the dynamics of an earthquake source following the formation of a main rupture within the rock mass. Keywords: earthquake source, main shock, relaxation, deactivation coefficient, proper time, inverse problem.
title: On dependence of the source deactivation factor on the magnitude of main earthquake shock

summary: Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two.
title: Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba-CNN for MODIS Spectral-Temporal Unmixing with Endmember Variability Modeling

summary: Open Data Analysis Tool for Science and Engineering (ODAT-SE) is an open-source Python framework for inverse problems that are solved by repeated forward simulations. It succeeds 2DMAT, which was developed for surface-structure analysis with quantum-beam diffraction and has since been applied to other fields. In version 3, the search algorithms were separated from the application-specific solvers, which became independent packages, and the software was renamed; this paper describes the current version 4.0. The framework connects optimization and sampling algorithms to solvers through a common interface for parameter mapping, constraints, and objective evaluation, so that an existing simulation code can be used with any of the algorithms. Relative to the previously published 2DMAT, it provides two-level MPI parallelism, which distributes candidate evaluations over processes and each evaluation over a parallel solver, checkpoint and continuation facilities, random search, global optimizers from SciPy, tensor-train optimization, and a Bayesian workflow that estimates partition-function ratios, model evidence, effective noise levels, and marginal posterior distributions. We validate the Bayesian workflow against closed-form results for a linear regression, benchmark tensor-train optimization on continuous, binary, and mixed-integer problems, and verify the two-level parallelization by the same optimum for all process decompositions. Taking up the positron-diffraction example of the 2DMAT paper, the workflow identifies the correlated structural solutions and an effective noise scale close to the imposed perturbation, while exposing incomplete convergence of symmetry-related mode weights. Solver packages, templates, and a gallery of examples support the use of the framework as a general platform for inverse-problem analysis.
title: ODAT-SE: A modular and parallel framework for simulation-based inverse problems

summary: This paper unifies six decades of image modeling, evolving from handcrafted mathematical tractable priors to solve inverse problems in imaging to data-driven deep foundation image models for both image generation and solving inverse problems, under a common Bayesian framework that formulates image modeling as an implicit or explicit probabilistic characterization of a data manifold. Every image restoration or generative task fundamentally seeks to answer the same question: What makes an image look like a real image? In the Bayesian framework, this question is encapsulated by the prior probability density p(x), or its more optimization-friendly counterpart, the log-prior log p(x). While early works in solving inverse problems, such as Tikhonov, Total Variation (TV), and Non-local priors relied on explicit handcrafted definitions of log prior to model local smoothness, modern techniques, such as Plug-and-Play (PnP) priors and Denoising Diffusion models, are rooted in algorithmic uncoupling and implicit manifold learning that apply to both inverse problems and conditional image generation. By grounding imaging inverse problems and conditional image generation under a single mathematical engine: the gradient of the log-prior, or the Stein Score Function, we bridge the gap between signal processing and machine learning communities, turning what seems like parallel developments into a single, evolution of image modeling from handcrafted analytical models to models learned from big data, demonstrating that the pursuit of the denoising score is the common thread connecting variational optimization (in MAP estimation) to posterior sampling (in modern foundation image models).
title: Image Modeling: From Handcrafted Priors to Foundation Image Models

summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.
title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification

summary: Transferring semantically typed tokens between heterogeneous blockchains (e.g. EVM and Cosmos ecosystems) raises two problems: semantic mixing, the loss of a token's domainspecific meaning in transit (e.g., CO2 removals issued under different methodologies), and atomicity despite divergent consensus and timing assumptions. We propose a bridge that addresses both. A deterministic indicator identity derived from cryptographic commitments, mirrored in class registries on both chains and checked at mint time, preventing semantic mixing by construction. For atomicity, we extend hash time-locked contracts (HTLCs) from two-party exchange to single-owner transfer with an automatic callback that burns the source escrow after a destination claim, and a protocol-minimum bounty that makes the fallback burn incentive-compatible even against adversarial senders. We machine-check the protocol's invariants with TLC (supply conservation fails without the rational-monitor assumption and holds with it) and validate a bidirectional prototype on Polygon and Neutron mainnets over Axelar GMP: fully automatic transfers with a median end-to-end latency of 97 s over 50 Polygon to Neutron transfers across 7 days (all completed by the on-chain automatic callback) and 93 s in the reverse direction, and semantic-validation overhead below 0.4% of messaging cost. We also document the integration failure modes of Cosmos originated messaging, whose dominant operational risk proves to be relay eligibility rather than latency.
title: An EVM-Cosmos Bridge for Atomic, Semantic-Preserving Transfer of Environmental Tokens

summary: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.
title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use

summary: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.
title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data

summary: A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.
title: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features

summary: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.
title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution

summary: Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.
title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training

summary: For a deterministic sequence of normal unital completely positive maps on a von Neumann algebra, convergence of normal states, loss of memory, and convergence of Cesàro averages are different properties. This paper separates these properties in the predual norm and identifies the precise role of composition order. Uniform loss of memory for right-appended products on the predual implies uniform convergence to a normal state without any compactness or trace assumption; the convergence rate is bounded by the image diameter. In contrast, on every infinite-dimensional $σ$-finite von Neumann algebra there are right-appended products with pointwise loss of memory but no convergent normal-state trajectory, even though all nontrivial state images equal a fixed compact line segment. Consequently, finite dimensionality is characterized by the universal implication from pointwise backward memory loss to mixing. An attained normal-functional minorization coefficient extends the common-lower-bound construction for matrix channels to arbitrary von Neumann algebras and yields quantitative contraction and unique normal entrance laws. Further results distinguish pointwise from uniform relaxation, Cesàro convergence from mixing, fixed-start from time-uniform contraction, and stationary from moving asymptotic states. As an application, inhomogeneous transfer states on spin chains, including matrix product states, are shown to have a unique thermodynamic limit, uniformly in the boundary condition, with an arbitrary von Neumann algebra as bond algebra; boundary dependence and correlations are controlled by the same product coefficients. All counterexamples are explicit and extend to algebras of types I, II, and III.
title: Ergodicity, memory loss, and directional stability on von Neumann algebras

summary: Fracture in food can be undesired during production and transportation but also intended during cutting, grinding or mastication. The associated peak load, the deformation at failure and the resulting fragment geometry are all product properties. This work condenses the modeling of such fracture into a physically rigorous recipe that considers the practical constraints imposed by finite element simulations where necessary and applies idealized theoretical assessments where applicable. Cooled dark chocolate serves as a reproducible model material. Two well-established modeling frameworks for Griffith-type brittle fracture are assessed at an affordable spatial discretization: a sharp-interface and a diffuse phase-field approach. The assessment covers the choice of numerical framework, its discretization and a staged identification of the model parameters. Each parameter is identified from the loading stage that governs it: elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force, and the phase-field width last. The phase-field width interferes with the structural response, crack curvature and stress fields, depending on its lower bound set by the affordable spatial resolution. Elastic slope, peak force and crack path therefore cannot be met practically by a single parameter set. The objective must be fixed for the calibration of the model parameters and reported together with the numerical parameters and the boundary value problem.
title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate

summary: Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. This study developed OpenGray, a benchmark of planning tasks with known correct decisions. Materials and methods: OpenGray adds tasks with known answers to the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset, including two contradictions with dose goals proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal. Four systems, from a rule-based planning script to a full LLM agent, were evaluated on 30 patients, the LLM-based ones with a commercial (Terra) and a local (Ministral 3 8B) LLM. Decisions, achieved dose, problem recognition, and technical failures were recorded and also read from logs of 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of SAGE, a clinical LLM agent. Results: With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent had decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, respectively, yet escalated only 50% (95% confidence interval, 25-75%) and 25% (10-40%) of overlap contradictions, which required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met. In four SAGE runs, one goal failed at every attempt; the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping. Conclusions: Favorable aggregate scores concealed specific decision failures. Planning agents should be evaluated on their decisions as well as their dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.
title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents

summary: Several apparently distinct formulations of the charged-lepton mass relation $p_2/e_1^2 = 2/3$ share a common algebraic object: the ratio of flavor-breaking to flavor-symmetric amplitude components on an internal family space. We show that (i) the relation expressed as a Fourier-mode constraint on Shulga's compact cycle, (ii) the same relation as a Descartes curvature condition in the sense of Kocik, and (iii) the Soddy completion of the resulting circle configuration are related by exact algebra, with no approximations. The Soddy completion defines a companion scale $F^2 = α^2 μ_\star$ with $α= \sqrt{3/2} - 1$ and $μ_\star = \sum_\ell m_\ell$; identifying this scale with $\bar{m}^{\rm MS}_s(μ_\star)$ yields a light-quark mass cascade with the ratio $m_d/m_s = 5/2 - \sqrt{6}$. Combined with the leading Gatto-Sartori-Tonin relation, this gives the down-sector Cabibbo seed $\sqrt{m_d/m_s} = \sqrt{3/2} - 1 = 0.22474\ldots$, numerically close to the measured $|V_{us}| = 0.22503 \pm 0.00068$ ($0.4σ$). A full CKM evaluation requires the up-sector phase correction, which we defer. The correspondence is testable by future lattice QCD+QED determinations of $m_d/m_s$; explicit failure modes are listed.
title: Descartes Curvature Geometry, Compact-Cycle Amplitudes, and the GST Cabibbo Seed

summary: A user history can admit multiple plausible next interactions, yet conventional sequential recommenders produce a single deterministic ranking. While diffusion models offer a natural way to sample alternative continuations, we show that existing target-item diffusion recommenders often suffer from severe sampling collapse, producing nearly identical outputs across independent draws. We identify two ubiquitous design choices that promote this collapse: joint learning of the latent space and denoiser, and in-trajectory supervision via discrete losses. To address these failure modes, we introduce DARTS (Diverse and Accurate Recommendation Through Sampling), a three-stage latent diffusion framework that explicitly decouples representation learning, generative modeling, and discrete ranking by learning and freezing the latent space before diffusion training and postponing ranking supervision to the final decoding stage. We further characterize sampling diversity using complementary measures of variation before and after decoding, and use posterior-predictive aggregation to exploit this diversity at inference. Across three Amazon Reviews 2023 categories, DARTS preserves substantially greater sampling diversity while outperforming strong sequential, generative-retrieval, and diffusion baselines by 7-12% on standard ranking metrics. Aggregating multiple samples further improves ranking accuracy at a fixed slate size.
title: When Diffusion Recommenders Stop Sampling: Preserving Generative Diversity

summary: Disasters are not merely natural phenomena; they are socially constructed events that emerge from the interaction between hazardous events and the vulnerable conditions of exposed communities. Floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones, wildfires, droughts, and extreme weather events continue to cause widespread human, material, economic, and environmental losses across the globe. As climate change intensifies hazard events, urbanization concentrates populations in vulnerable areas, and technological systems become increasingly complex and interdependent, the need for sophisticated disaster management capabilities has never been greater. This book explores the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in disaster management. It examines how AI technologies—including machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, robotics, and expert systems—are being applied across all phases of the disaster management cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. The integration of AI with remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, cloud computing, and real-time analytics offers unprecedented opportunities for predicting, preparing for, responding to, and recovering from disasters. The book is organized into eleven chapters that progressively build the reader's understanding of this interdisciplinary field. Chapter 1 establishes the foundational concepts of disasters, the disaster management cycle, and the evolution of disaster management technologies. Chapter 2 introduces the fundamentals of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and neural network architectures, with a focus on their relevance to disaster applications. Chapter 3 examines AI based disaster risk assessment and hazard mapping, integrating geospatial information,  environmental observations, and computational models. Chapters 4 through 8 address specific disaster types: floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones and extreme weather events, and wildfires, droughts, and climate-related disasters. Each chapter presents AI applications, case studies, numerical examples, and integrated frameworks tailored to the unique characteristics of these hazards. Chapter 9 explores the synergy between remote sensing, GIS, and AI for disaster mapping and damage assessment. Chapter 10 focuses on IoT, sensors, and real-time AI-based disaster monitoring, emphasizing edge computing, cloud platforms, and early-warning systems. Chapter 11 presents an integrated AI framework, case studies from India and internationally, performance evaluation metrics, challenges, research gaps, and future directions.    Throughout the book, a critical distinction is maintained: AI should not be viewed as a replacement for human judgment, field observations, engineering expertise, or disaster management experience. Rather, AI serves as a powerful complement—augmenting human capabilities, improving the speed and consistency of information processing, and supporting evidence-based forecasting, monitoring, response, and recovery. The most effective disaster management architecture integrates AI with hydrological and hydraulic modelling, seismology, structural engineering, geotechnical engineering, meteorological science, and institutional decision-making. The book emphasizes several cross-cutting themes. First, the relationship between hazard, vulnerability, exposure, and risk provides the analytical foundation for disaster risk assessment. The formula Risk = (Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure) / Capacity demonstrates that risk can be reduced through strategic interventions that decrease vulnerability and exposure or increase capacity. Second, data quality, algorithmic bias, infrastructure requirements, trust deficits,  privacy concerns, capacity gaps, interoperability problems, and regulatory uncertainty must all be addressed for AI to achieve its full potential. Third, expl
title: AI IN DISASTER MANAGEMENT

summary: The logarithmically averaged two-point Chowla conjecture was proved by Tao and quantitatively improved by Helfgott–Radziwiłł and Pilatte, through a dilation identity followed by a spectral bound for a divisibility operator. On the generalised Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (GEH), Bombieri's asymptotic sieve turns the twin prime conjecture into a Chowla-type statement on almost primes, and Tao remarked that this restriction destroys the multiplicativity the Chowla arguments rely on. We make this remark a theorem. We define a class of dilation–spectral certificates containing the Helfgott–Radziwiłł and Pilatte certificates adapted to the shift 2, with arbitrary smooth, rough or mixed dilators up to x κ , and prove that every such certificate has resolution >> η min(1, η/κ) log x on twin-type parity (Theorem A). The loss is the factor 1/log x η that two-sided roughness costs on every edge. To state what such a certificate would have to resolve, we write the Bombieri–Tao reformulation as an exact, numerically testable identity for ∑ n≤X Λ(n)Λ(n+2)/n in terms of a logarithmic parity defect ρ(X) of the Liouville function on almost-prime pairs (Theorem B), and show that on GEH the joint parity of rough pairs is governed by the twin parameter alone (Theorem C). A road map (Figure 1) summarises the structure. New in version 0.6. Section 6.3, "The roughness ceiling of known mechanisms". Theorem A holds uniformly in the roughness level z, so dilation–spectral certificates can resolve parity only on z-rough integers with z ≤ exp(O(√log x)) (Corollary 6.11, a theorem). Two further remarks analyse specific arguments: Tao's entropy-decrement iteration, which reaches z ≤ (log x) o(1) , and the recent Lü–Wang–Wu argument for μ(p+2) (arXiv:2610.20242, unrefereed), which reaches z ≤ exp((log x) c ) with c < 1/5 and cannot start at x η . These remarks concern those specific proofs, not every argument of their kind. All known mechanisms stop far below the roughness x η that Bombieri's parity parameter requires. The code bundle adds the scripts entropy_test.py and bilinear_probe.py with their data up to x = 10 8 . New in version 0.7. Theorem E, a rigorous limitation theorem for entropy-decrement arguments. We define entropy-decrement certificates by the ingredients of Tao's argument: an entropy budget, the decrement inequality, and a decoupling step that uses only boundedness and sparsity, so variance-sensitive variants are included. Two explicit sharpness constructions show that such certificates can resolve twin-type parity only on z-rough integers with z ≤ (log x) O(ε 4 ) at precision ε. Together with Corollary 6.11, two rows of the roughness-ceiling table are now theorems. The code bundle adds pellet_check.py, which verifies Pellet's formula μ(f) = (−1) deg f χ(disc f) over F 3 and F 5 , the function-field mechanism behind the Sawin–Shusterman twin prime theorem, which has no known integer analogue. New in version 0.8. Appendix D.5, "Map of explored routes and the hypothesis ledger": a figure of every route explored in the project with its status (theorem, theorem in a model, analysis, numerical), and a ledger of bold hypotheses H1–H7 with their tests. Two are notable. H3, a finite parity linear program over many patterns with positivity and one-sided parity constraints, is refuted in the model by an explicit witness: any two-point parity counterfeit extends independently to larger patterns, so these constraints alone cannot exclude δ = 0. H6, a base- p analogue of Pellet's formula, shows no correlation between λ( n ) and the function-field Möbius of the digit polynomial at x ≈ 10 8 (all | z | ≤ 1.65). The code bundle adds parity_lp.py, h6_digits.py and the map generator. New in version 0.9. Four new results. (1) Corollar
title: Why expansion methods for Chowla do not reach twin primes: a method-limitation theorem and an explicit parity compiler

summary: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.
title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions

summary: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning

summary: We examine conditional charged-multiplicity fluctuations at fixed multiparton interaction (MPI) count in retained PYTHIA proton-proton samples at centre-of-mass energies of 2.76, 7, and 13 TeV. Charged particles satisfy |eta| < 0.8 and 0.15 < pT < 20 GeV/c. In the historical colour-reconnection (CR)-labelled baseline samples, the CR-ON conditional mean is smaller by a larger fraction than the standard deviation: the absolute width is smaller, while the coefficient of variation is larger in every retained matched MPI bin. Effective lifetime/decay settings and their per-run correspondence are unverified for this baseline, so these comparisons do not establish that CR alone causes the observed differences or their energy dependence. A separately documented 13 TeV comparison using the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) CP5 tune, with equal non-CR physics settings and particle data across the ON/OFF pair, exhibits the same absolute-versus-relative width ordering. Retained independent Monash and A14 samples also show this pattern, subject to historical production-record limitations. A comparison with mean-transverse-momentum data from A Large Ion Collider Experiment (ALICE) and simulated activity estimators provides final-state context within the stated particle-definition and provenance limits.
title: Color-Reconnection Effects on the nMPI-Nch Conditional Multiplicity Fluctuations in PYTHIA 8 pp Collisions

summary: Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training pairs.
title: ALADDIN: Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping

summary: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. We study how this field evolves when the covariates of individual units move as a diffusion and the outcome attached to each unit changes according to its own dynamics. Under mild regularity we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(Σ\nabla^2 m_t)$, the trace of the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the instantaneous covariance $Σ$ of the covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome. The equation is a regression-theoretic reading of a classical transport law, and it yields a Feynman-Kac representation of $m_t$ along reversed covariate paths. We connect the Hessian appearing in the equation to the Hessian estimated by quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$ exactly) and to the leading bias of kernel smoothers. For binary outcomes governed by bistable replicator dynamics with imitation among units with similar covariates, the closed equation is of Nagumo type, its planar travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, and a single logistic regression of the outcome on covariates and time identifies the ratio of diffusion to reaction and the direction of invasion. We discuss identification under panel versus repeated cross-sectional designs and a two-stage estimation strategy, and we illustrate the results with simulations.
title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification

summary: We develop a multifidelity black-box variational inference (MF-BBVI) approach for PDE-constrained Bayesian inverse problems in which forward solves are expensive and PDE gradients are unavailable. The method is built on score-function estimators for the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which avoid differentiation through the PDE model but are known to suffer from high variance. To address this high variance, we employ multifidelity approximate control-variate estimators that combine a small number of high-fidelity samples with a larger number of low-fidelity samples to reduce estimator variance and the number of high-fidelity evaluations required for optimization. We further develop a PDE-derivative-free second-order optimization strategy based on both gradient and Hessian score-function estimators. For low-fidelity model generation, we propose an on-the-fly strategy that builds and adaptively updates a reduced-order model (ROM) as the variational distribution evolves throughout the optimization. We investigate strategies for adapting the ROM and estimating the approximate control-variate gains, examining tradeoffs between estimator bias, variance reduction, and computational cost. The resulting approach facilitates derivative-free variational inference for large-scale inverse problems through a reduction in overall computational cost. We demonstrate the method on four numerical examples: a linear benchmark with an exact posterior and three PDE-constrained inverse problems.
title: Multifidelity variational inference for derivative-free PDE-constrained inverse problems

summary: We present a survey of approaches to Bayesian inference with simulator forward models, focusing on settings with prohibitively expensive simulators. In this domain, Bayesian optimization-based methods have emerged as the most promising approach. We unify existing methods into a general framework, enabling consistent reasoning about shared algorithmic structure across the fragmented literature. Within this framework, we identify the primary design choices and perform a systematic empirical comparison of their effects on inference efficiency in terms of required simulation budget. A key result of our study is that inference efficiency is often dominated by the choice of surrogate-model response variable, as it directly governs the complexity of the modeled function. Specifically, we demonstrate that the prevalent scalar log-likelihood is a poor response variable, as it discards crucial information. Based on this insight, we introduce the concept of custom \emph{proxy variables}: transformations of simulator outputs engineered to retain more information and provide smoother response surfaces, substantially improving inference efficiency over standard response variables. We provide actionable guidance and a numerically robust Julia package to facilitate practical adoption of Bayesian optimization for simulator inverse problems.
title: Bayesian Inference of Expensive Simulators: Survey and Comparison of Design Choices

summary: QIGONG BREATHING AND INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE NEUROFEEDBACK COUPLING AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition that constructs a falsifiable, explicitly nonclinical research program joining measured breathing tasks, cardiorespiratory and EEG feedback, and isolated microscale actuator surrogates. The central problem is not whether breathing changes heart-rate variability - that has established ordinary physiological explanations - but whether a proposed feedback architecture adds independently measurable predictive or benchtop-control value after breathing rate, phase, expectancy, ordinary cardiorespiratory dynamics, sensor calibration, stimulus timing and strong conventional controllers have been fairly matched. The primary hypothesis is deliberately narrow. A prospective factorial design separates a preregistered breathing condition from an isolated, non-human phantom-drive condition. Its interaction term, order effects, washout, hierarchical sampling units, pressure-related mechanisms and full-episode denominators are subjected to masked scheduling, matched sham sensory cues, covariance-aware uncertainty and independent laboratory reconstruction. Any apparent signal explained by paced breathing or cue entrainment is treated as a legitimate negative result. A bench interaction is not evidence of physiological effects from actual acupuncture in a person. Thirty mathematically differentiated research plates address factorial contrasts, hierarchical estimands, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, ECG event genealogy, pressure-respiration transfer, spectral coherence, lag and phase, multiple comparisons, uncertainty covariance, causal identification, feedback latency, safe-state projection, isolated charge and thermal constraints, abstention and provenance. Across 82 chapters and 410 separately paginated scientific investigations, the book examines operational breathing definitions, reference instruments, EEG and ECG artifacts, blinded feedback protocols, mechanical and electrical phantoms, strong ordinary competitors, statistics, safety vetoes and reproducible handoff. Two hundred full-page Research Gates place their complete falsifiable research question in large deep-navy type, followed by an independently measurable outcome, adverse experiment, conventional physical rival and stopping rule. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct successor objects ranging from calibration bridges and sham credibility tests to independent hardware vetoes, covariance sentinels, multisite reference capsules and protected null-result archives. An accompanying Excel index links formulas, chapters, Gates, candidate objects, citations and explicit evidence limitations. This work reports no executed integrated experiments, in-human needling, electrical stimulation, clinical efficacy, diagnosis or regulatory authorization. Its three STARLI mother-volume DOIs establish author research-method ancestry. Thirteen separately identified external research and metrology DOIs support established measurement, breathing physiology, neurofeedback reporting, uncertainty and statistical methodology, not the novel combined hypothesis. The 777-page layout, formula-clearance checks and 200 Gate color checks were automated; recurring editorial phrasing remains and full independent scientific peer review has not taken place. title: kmhelpers: A Python toolkit for automated management of genomic indexes

summary: Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.
title: LM-DSB: A Lightweight Multi-agent System for Automated Daily Safety Bulletin Generation in Construction

summary: TRUSTWORTHY MANUFACTURING AND DIGITAL QUALITY PASSPORTS FOR BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT Manufacturing Evidence x Digital Traceability x Quality Release This 770-page Research Working Edition develops a falsification-oriented, nonclinical architecture for proving whether every biomedical micro/nanorobot product or batch can be linked to sufficient material, tool, model, process, test and failure evidence for an independent team to reconstruct its release rationale. It distinguishes record completeness from product qualification and treats physical identity, typed provenance, signature status, version compatibility, raw functional evidence, uncertainty, recall and retirement as separate scientific objects. The monograph contains 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 single-page investigations, 200 differentiated Research Gates and 33 genuinely distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. The minimum demonstrator conceals three critical evidence gaps inside a signed passport and tests whether an independent audit refuses release without original-author assistance. A critical missing ancestor, ambiguous product identity, unverifiable signature, incompatible model evidence or unreplayable release decision is a hard veto. This is a prospective scientific architecture, not an executed clinical or regulatory study. It does not claim in-body safety, therapeutic efficacy, regulatory approval or clinical benefit. DOI-linked publications support component methods and boundaries; they do not validate the integrated F25 system. Technical profile: 770 pages; approximately 166,832 English words; 30 formula families; 82 chapters; 410 single-page studies; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 22 DOI records; navigable bookmarks; sixfold QA. The monograph contains 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 single-page investigations, 200 differentiated Research Gates and 33 genuinely distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. The minimum demonstrator conceals three critical evidence gaps inside a signed passport and tests whether an independent audit refuses release without original-author assistance. A critical missing ancestor, ambiguous product identity, unverifiable signature, incompatible model evidence or unreplayable release decision is a hard veto. This is a prospective scientific architecture, not an executed clinical or regulatory study. It does not claim in-body safety, therapeutic efficacy, regulatory approval or clinical benefit. DOI-linked publications support component methods and boundaries; they do not validate the integrated F25 system. Technical profile: 770 pages; approximately 166,832 English words; 30 formula families; 82 chapters; 410 single-page studies; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 22 DOI records; navigable bookmarks; sixfold QA. Author: Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli STARLI Research Institute XXXIV / Flagship 25 Join the STARLI Research Community Explore more than 100 interdisciplinary research themes and follow the evolving STARLI Research Gate community: https://zenodo.org/communities/starli-research-gate/

The split‑Gibbs null result therefore has a further candidate explanation that DP1 cannot separate. DPS is unaffected. No file of earlier versions has changed. A pre-specified pilot testing whether a blindness-risk score computed before any target data are seen ranks the realised blindness (undetected and uncovered error) of diffusion-prior inference on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access. Study DP-A: weak attenuation (F = 32,000), 240 errors × 20 bases. Study DP-B: bounded-reach control, 120 errors × 20 bases. Two samplers: split-Gibbs plug-and-play (primary) and diffusion posterior sampling (secondary). It follows the learned (VAE) pilot, arXiv:2610.28155 (reproducibility package doi:10.5281/zenodo.23392686). The analysis plan, decision rules and fixed result sentences were approved by the author, and predictions and calibration were committed by SHA-256 hash, before any trial. The plan was not lodged with an external registry, so the study is described as pre-specified; the files named PREREG_… are that plan (their names, and the word "pre-registered" inside the hashed plan and the dated log, are kept unchanged so that the recorded hashes still match). Under the plan’s pre-specified reading, the response was not adequate for either sampler in either study, so the null result for the learned score does not separate the learned prior from this approximation.
