title: BLINDSET diffusion-prior blind-set pilot: analysis plan, code, frozen predictions, trial records and results

summary: This version (v1.4) extends the reproducibility package for “Before the weights: a validated admission gate for data-derived decision inputs, demonstrated on aggregate inward FDI” (Results in Engineering, manuscript RINENG-D-26-21905). It adds the records of a prospective, prespecified, synthetic-only benchmark comparing the frozen admission gate (G) with two simpler calibrated admission rules: a Ridge-only rule (A) and a single-split rule (B). The principal finding is unfavourable to the gate. At the smaller planted effect (δ = 0.005), G admitted 27 of 50 cases, A admitted 26 of 50, and B admitted 49 of 50. None of the three rules admitted any of 50 synthetic null or 40 persistence-matched null candidates at their calibrated operating points. The prespecified outcome labels were “No statistically resolved difference” for A and “Evidence favouring the comparator” for B. The comparison is conditional on the tested synthetic designs. It does not establish equal population-level false-admission rates, demonstrate downstream decision improvements, or test genuinely environment-dependent planted effects. The deposit contains the benchmark protocol, implementation, calibration records, seed registry, 190-cell execution return, reduction report, execution history, and independent verification records. Certain operational records have been anonymised to protect identifying information. The included anonymisation map links the public files to their original hash-bound verification records. The public reproduction procedure independently reproduces the scientific reduction, with its documented protocol-hash substitution. The previously published v1.3 record remains unchanged. Consult README.md inside the archive for the reproduction instructions, scientific limitations, and relationship between the public derivative and the verified originals.
title: Before the Weights: Reproducibility package for a validated admission gate for data-derived inputs to mineral-resource decision support

summary: This research investigates recurring inconsistencies, context retention failures, and ineffective error correction in long-term interactions between humans and large language models (LLMs). Using a retrospective dataset of 1,271 ChatGPT conversations comprising 26,949 user–assistant messages , the study examines how AI systems maintain conversational context, respond to corrections, follow established instructions, and represent the status of completed tasks. A systematic screening process identified 495 potential feedback signals across 192 conversations. From these, 26 anonymized case studies were assembled to examine observable behavioral patterns, including contradictory responses, task deviation, unsupported claims of completed actions, loss of previously established constraints, and repeated errors following user correction. The study introduces context-state mismatch as an operational framework for examining discrepancies between the conversational record and an AI assistant's subsequent responses or claims. It distinguishes directly observable failures from user-reported concerns and cases requiring further verification. The findings highlight important challenges in conversational reliability, transparency, instruction adherence, and long-horizon human–AI collaboration. The paper proposes evaluation methods involving correction retention, independent verification, and tool-action accountability to improve the reliability of future AI systems. As a single-user observational study, the research does not claim to establish population-wide failure rates or definitive internal causes. Instead, it contributes original longitudinal evidence and a reproducible framework for investigating persistent limitations in LLM-assisted workflows.
title: Context-State Mismatch and Repair Failures in Long-Horizon Human–LLM Interaction

summary: Version 3 research revision. We study the part of a sensor field that remains covered after every failure in a prescribed downward-closed family. The model includes independent contact failures, weighted failure budgets and losses of entire fault domains. For a convex sensor cover with nerve N, we express the surviving region by a complex on the maximal faces of N: a collection of maximal faces is a simplex exactly when its common contact set cannot fail. This is a coverage formulation of classical nerve and Dowker duality, for which we give explicit comparison maps and prove naturality under increasing failure families. For n closed planar disks, all maximal nerve faces are witnessed by at most n^2 circle points. Exact rational sign tests consequently construct the full two-skeleton of the dual model without enumerating the original nerve or the coalition shadow. A separate Lipschitz margin theorem gives continuous coverage certificates for prescribed triangulated targets under the same failure rules. Recomputing five supplied fields completes the previously unfinished dense example: its two-fold covered region has Betti numbers (5,6), calculated from a dual complex with 130 vertices and independently checked boundary rank. The implementation, inputs, exact arithmetic conventions and verification records are supplied.
title: Sensor Coverage under Structured Failures: Dual Nerve Models and Exact Geometry

summary: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.
title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs

summary: This paper sets out what a sustained federal research and investment agenda would need to include to close that gap--not within a single budget cycle, but over the decade such an undertaking will realistically require. It identifies where the gap is most pronounced today: in the methods needed to verify and certify components of uncertain origin, in the foundational hardware research that has long been underfunded relative to software, in the physical infrastructure researchers need to test systems at scale, and in the workforce required to build and sustain all of it. Robotics should not be treated merely as a downstream beneficiary of a broader artificial intelligence investment strategy. It constitutes its own supply chain, with its own points of failure, and merits its own sustained federal commitment.
title: Securing the Robotics Supply Chain

summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.
title: Escaping Path Mirages in Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

summary: Military installation energy readiness depends on having sufficient resources to sustain mission-critical loads throughout a prolonged utility outage. This paper develops a method to help operators manage energy resources during normal grid-connected operation while preserving islanded readiness. A robust viability kernel identifies combinations of battery energy, fuel, and load-shifting capability sufficient to sustain critical load under uncertain demand and photovoltaic generation. A probability bound translates stochastic generator start failures and recovery into a deterministic generator count selected to meet a specified availability requirement at islanding. Case studies for a fourteen-day islanding requirement at 0.999 islanding-entry availability show that advance warning of an outage can be used to prepare resources to meet a higher readiness requirement before islanding begins. The case studies further demonstrate that economic-only operation and the evaluated fixed battery reserve policy can fail to sustain critical load for the required duration, whereas enforcing the resource-dependent requirement preserves readiness at a modest increase in modeled grid-connected operating cost. These results demonstrate how active resource management can preserve long-duration energy readiness. The framework also helps commanders understand how readiness changes with operating conditions, even when the available resources remain the same.
title: Readiness-Constrained Pre-Islanding Dispatch for Military Microgrids

summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
title: Agentic process evidence

summary: A ring is right pure semisimple if every right module is a direct sum of finitely generated modules, and the pure semisimplicity conjecture asserts that every such ring is of finite representation type. In this article, a division ring extension $H\subseteq T$ is constructed such that the bimodule ${}_HT_T$ has right dimension sequence $(1,2,2,2,\dots)$ and $T$ is infinite-dimensional as a left $H$-space. The division ring $T$ is the union of the fraction division rings of the nearest-neighbour quantum Laurent algebras with parameter $1/2$, and $H$ is the image of $T$ under a compatible family of conjugations. The extension is controlled by right bases of every length and by two-sided flags of adjacent division subrings, which identify all iterated right duals up to explicit twists. It follows that the triangular ring $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&T\\0&T\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is right pure semisimple but neither left pure semisimple nor of finite representation type, so that the pure semisimplicity conjecture fails.
title: A counterexample to the pure semisimplicity conjecture

summary: World action models (WAMs) increasingly couple internal visual or world representations with action generation, making their world-to-action pathways a critical yet poorly understood source of robustness. We investigate when perturbations to these internal representations actually become behaviorally consequential, and uncover a pronounced mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across visual K/V routes, while larger representation displacement does not reliably imply stronger control failure. Our analysis attributes this mismatch to the action-conditioned readout, where keys determine where action queries read and values determine what content they receive. This motivates an action-facing view of vulnerability, in which the effect of a perturbation depends on how it is routed into action generation rather than on representation-space magnitude alone. We instantiate this view with Tail-AV, a short-probe signal for identifying vulnerable routes, and operationalize it in PASA-KV, which selects action-facing K/V targets before training a fresh task-shared attack. Experiments across multiple WAM systems and a physical robot validate readout-informed target selection, demonstrate strong closed-loop attacks, and reveal substantial system-level differences in resistance.
title: PASA-KV: Attacking Action-Facing Visual Routes in World Action Models

summary: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.
title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed

summary: Planning at run time, as in robots that re-plan while they act, needs a planner that reads the PDDL its users write (durative actions, numeric resources, time windows, continuous change), answers quickly, and delivers only validated plans. Specialised planners are strong on individual fragments of PDDL, but they differ in coverage, latency and in what their failures mean. We study whether selecting heterogeneous engines from the semantics of each task can give broad coverage of PDDL, from STRIPS to PDDL+, while remaining competitive with specialised planners and making explicit what each answer guarantees. Kairos profiles each task to decide which of five engines apply (ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time steps for hybrid dynamics, lifted search) and schedules them under one budget of time and memory. Every candidate plan is checked by a validator independent of the planner's transformations, and "unsolvable" is reported only when a search whose exhaustion is a proof exhausts its space. On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites, Kairos solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, with the largest differences on numeric, temporal, PDDL3 and PDDL+ planning, and it also solves the most tasks at 100 ms and 1 s. Resampling over domains, the gain is above zero in six of the nine suites, while on classical planning against LAMA it is within the noise. A further 450 feature-oriented tasks and 26 one-feature probes show that Kairos handles all seventeen features probed, where no other planner evaluated handles more than eight. Ablations identify compressed temporal search and the novelty fallback as major contributors, and a comparison with VAL traces every disagreement to a PDDL+ convention or to a documented VAL defect. Planner and benchmark are open source.
title: Kairos: Semantics-Aware Orchestration of Planning Engines across Classical, Numeric, Temporal and Hybrid PDDL

summary: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.
title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning

summary: Skill-evolution methods typically analyze execution trajectories to guide agent skill refinement. However, policy updates can change the behavioral effects and marginal utility of an unchanged skill. Attribution based on earlier trajectories may therefore no longer reflect the skill's contribution under the updated policy. Moreover, trajectory failures can arise from multiple factors, making individual skill contributions difficult to isolate. We evaluate whether policy-update signals contain predictive information about changes in skill marginal utility. At fixed contexts from pre-update training rollouts, we measure how policy updates change the contrast in token preferences between skill and control conditions. Combining these interaction shifts with advantage estimates yields reward-directed readouts for diagnosing utility changes. The readouts reuse existing training rollouts and require only forward passes for single-step action scoring, without additional post-update rollout evaluation. Our experiments show that policy updates can alter skill marginal utility and that policy-update readouts carry diagnostic information for identifying skills with declining utility. Integrating readout-guided prioritization into skill evolution improves downstream performance while reducing policy and editor token consumption.
title: Before the Next Rollout: Diagnosing Skill Utility Shifts from Policy Updates

summary: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.
title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories

summary: Fight, flight, and relaxation describe bodily mobilisation and recovery but leave open how attention is selectively withheld or invested in discovery. This article examines ignoring and exploring as two modes of engagement whose neural and bodily organisation requires separate analysis. Ignoring reduces processing of particular information; exploring gathers information about something incompletely known. Evidence from distractor-suppression research indicates that ignoring is an organised, often learned and sometimes anticipatory form of neural selection. Research on curiosity, exploratory choice, and orienting relates exploration to motivated learning and arousal regulation, and shows that cardiac responses unfold in stages that distinguish information intake from preparation for action. The article separates attentional investment in an input from bodily mobilisation, which permits relaxed exploration, mobilised investigation, ignoring at ease, and ignoring under exertion. It distinguishes three ways of letting something pass (sensory filtering, nonreactivity to a noticed experience, and effortful suppression) that differ in what is recognised and in their bodily costs. Quiet readiness is defined in signal-detection terms as reduced interference from irrelevant inputs, preserved sensitivity to inputs whose relevance changes, a response criterion near its optimum, and bodily cost no greater than the task requires. Three failure profiles follow: rigid filtering (an overly conservative criterion), anxious vigilance (an overly liberal criterion at high cost), and distractible ease (weak suppression). Five hypotheses, each paired with a rival, are assigned to three staged studies. Implications for the M⁵ model of mindfulness are outlined. The framework is an agenda for testing, not a taxonomy of nervous-system states.
title: Ignoring and Exploring: Nervous System Engagement Beyond Fight, Flight, and Relaxation

summary: Borrowed Youth: Demographic Change and Multinational Location Advantage explains how national cohort succession and international recruitment become firm-specific location advantages over a production commitment. Home-linked relationships, recruitment shared across foreign affiliates and admission institutions determine attainable replacement labour. Version 3.33.0 clarifies the empirical bridge and journal exposition. The model-to-data mapping distinguishes accessible worker stocks and annual arrival flows from their discounted service values. Table 3 now leads with the main engineering-life comparison, followed by the accounting and common-support benchmarks. The country equal-pricing contrasts are expressed as conditional investment changes holding total measured international services fixed, with full covariance and uncertainty preserved. These transformations introduce no additional test, observation or regression. The discussion relates demographic succession to resource bundling, human-capital access and multinational portfolios. The exact AI declaration, including all figures, is preserved. Previously reported scientific results are preserved. The article supplies an explicit economic bridge from project value to expected investment allocation under stated choice, capital-size, duration and disclosure conditions. It distinguishes capital expenditure from accumulated assets, whose interpretation additionally depends on investment histories, depreciation and valuation changes. The retained capital-expenditure analysis uses the existing demographic construction and controls. There are 82 matched records from ten firms and 36 after fixed-effect support. The nuisance design has rank 33; the five focal regressors have rank three. Independent projection confirms this failure. No duration coefficient, interval or p-value is identified; the result is not a zero effect. The public module reconstructs the aggregate rank and supplies licensed rerun code without redistributing issuer rows. The existing engineering-life asset comparison remains: 317 allocations from 32 manufacturers in nine hosts, contrast -110.25 (95 percent interval -520.28 to 299.78; positive-direction p=0.724). Joint positive pricing and rotation are unestablished (p=0.763), and the familywise contradiction test does not reject (p=0.712). Existing Holm-adjusted block probabilities are 0.113, 0.085 and 0.656. All original estimates, covariance matrices, equations, formal results and six figures are preserved. These conditional associations do not identify recruitment-caused host choices. The held Nitra-Puebla appraisal supplies a EUR106-226 million residual strategic hurdle and 2,834 planned direct jobs. At a five-percent reference rate this is EUR2,959-6,308 per planned job-year. The retained frontier states the additional net productive service needed to cover an assigned share, excluding previously priced labour effects and without fitting a recruitment share. Cost-saving bounds distinguish fixed-life value improvement from a unique switch across lives. No new sources or observations were acquired. The manuscript has 9,920 counted words, a 172-word abstract and 23 full substantive pages before references; the main PDF has 41 pages and the appendix 137. Regression tables retain three-decimal probabilities, no significance stars and economic magnitudes. Counts include abstract, text, references and transparency; separately placed exhibits and the online appendix are excluded. Start with README.txt. Current article, appendix and complete LaTeX are directly downloadable. Three current verified ZIP blocks and nine frozen complementary archives reconstruct the exact 1,908-file replication tree with 1,907 checksum entries. Licensed WRDS rows are excluded; subscriber queries and public aggregate reconstruction are supplied. Third-party rights remain. Literature PDFs are linked rather than redistributed. ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI) were used in October 2026 for coding h
title: Borrowed Youth: Demographic Change and Multinational Location Advantage

summary: Anaerobic digestion (AD) requires close monitoring of key process variables, including pH, the ratio of volatile organic acids to alkaline buffer capacity and biogas production, to maintain biological stability and prevent process failure. While mechanistic frameworks such as the Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 are highly parameterised, computationally expensive, and difficult to calibrate for real-time applications, data-driven Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks offer a potentially more adaptable alternative. However, current data-driven approaches in AD are predominantly limited to single-output architectures that focus solely on production yields, as opposed to simultaneous prediction of vital stability indicators. Furthermore, industrial AD datasets are typically sparse and skewed toward steady-state operations. Baseline evaluations demonstrated this scarcity prevents standard algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost) and unaugmented LSTMs from recognising the transition to unstable operations, resulting in poor estimation of stability indicators. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a novel generative data augmentation framework using an LSTM-beta-Variational Autoencoder coupled with a multi-output LSTM (MO-LSTM) soft sensor. By synthesising physically valid sequences of these transitions to unstable operations from one year of full-scale plant data, the method safely populates sparse regions of the feature space. Trained on this augmented dataset, the MO-LSTM achieved robust simultaneous estimation across all targets. This approach mitigates data sparsity, providing a basis for hybrid mechanistic-data-driven modelling and early-warning soft sensors in industrial bioprocesses.
title: Multi-output LSTM soft sensors for industrial anaerobic co-digestion using LSTM-beta-VAE generative data augmentation

summary: A streaming estimator must compute from the evidence that fits in memory. We determine when storing an accurate mean is easier than computing it. For Gaussian mean estimation over the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we establish the minimax rate under squared error with $K$ persistent states, a known horizon, and a public time index: $\min\{1, K^{-2/d}+\frac{d}{n} (1+\frac{\log(ed)}{1+(\log K)/d})\}$. Unrestricted computation followed by $K$-level encoding has rate $\min\{1,d/n+K^{-2/d}\}$. At a fixed sufficiently small error, statistically optimal sample size therefore requires order $d\log d$ working bits, while order $d$ bits suffice to store the answer. The lower bound tracks repeated state compression through an entropy potential obtained by Gaussian smoothing. A matching construction combines a multiscale modular counter with workspace reused across coordinate groups. In one dimension, it attains the terminal rate $n^{-1}+K^{-2}$. Any fixed confidence requirement that the realized loss not exceed the zero baseline preserves these rates. Increasing confidence creates a further memory requirement: at fixed nontrivial risk in every fixed dimension, failure probability $e^{-γn}$ requires and permits order $\log n$ working states for sufficiently small fixed $γ>0$. In the scalar problem, a fixed terminal alphabet suffices under the same protection. These bounds separate the memory needed to represent an answer from the memory needed to accumulate evidence and validate a decision.
title: The Cost of Working Memory in Streaming Mean Estimation

summary: An effective agent memory system should adapt to a user's history and task requirements. Human-annotated supervision can guide this adaptation by providing feedback for evaluating and improving memory designs. Yet suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories, and manually constructing QA pairs and supporting evidence is costly. We introduce MemSteer, which turns unlabeled user histories into question-answer (QA) supervision with supporting evidence for memory-design optimization. MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, while source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the resulting annotations. To study the utility of this supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that this supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimization. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 and 6.6 points without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench, while new-user experiments demonstrate continued design optimization using supervision generated from the target histories.
title: MemSteer: Turning User Histories into Supervision for Agent Memory Optimization

summary: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
title: AtomTree: A Hierarchical Framework for State-Aware Embodied Instruction Following with LLMs

summary: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is not merely long-sequence modeling. Once the volume is packed, sequence order no longer encodes the geometry of the sample---so a positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can learn the memory layout rather than the object. This is a general failure mode for attention over packed geometric data. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and indexes every query-key interaction with axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates rather than packed positions. Because the rotation is applied before a block is summarized, the query-to-summary logit remains a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements; compressed global context therefore stays spatially interpretable after packing, instead of collapsing to anonymous pooled content. We measure the failure mode directly. On a controlled synthetic task---train on one packing, change only the memory order of the tokens, hold the physical labeling rule fixed---learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE solve the training layout perfectly yet collapse under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact throughout. The same coordinate system carries to real data: on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, with controls isolating the coordinate system, not encoder capacity, as the source of the gain. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while supplying the long-range context windowing cannot---so the operator is not only correct but trainable at scale.
title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention

summary: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.
title: When More Planning Hurts: Learned Planners for World Models

summary: Long-horizon consistency is essential for video world models, yet it becomes difficult to maintain once observed content falls outside the context window. Existing memory mechanisms either retrieve history as implicit context, which remains constrained by context capacity and entangles static and dynamic information or consolidate history into explicit global representations, which struggle to model evolving dynamics and accumulate geometric errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce \textbf{GROME}, a novel factorized memory framework that augments video world models for long-horizon coherence across both static scenes and dynamic entities. GROME operates via three synergistic components: 1)~\emph{Static-Dynamic Factorization} decouples historical evidence into static and dynamic components, preserving static scene geometry and dynamic entity states separately; 2)~\emph{Local Memory Retrieval} selects spatially aligned static history to eliminate geometric drift alongside the latest dynamic entity states to ensure temporal continuity; 3)~\emph{Training-Free Memory Injection} seamlessly grounds the factorized memory into video world models via their native conditioning pathways. Experiments on long-horizon revisit scenarios demonstrate that GROME substantially enhances scene persistence and dynamic entity fidelity over existing methods, all while preserving the visual quality and controllability of the frozen backbone without additional training. Beyond self-rollouts, GROME readily accommodates external observations as plug-and-play memory, unlocking flexible and controllable video continuation and scene exploration.
title: GROME: GROunding Factorized MEmory into Video World Models

summary: Gravitational observations can leave material properties undetermined in two different ways: distinct states can have the same total source, and distinct spacetime histories can have the same retained observations. We organize these inverse problems in general relativity through a property-level identifiability criterion, with applications to stars and black hole candidates. Two ideal massless gases illustrate equal-source ambiguity: their temperatures differ by a factor of $(8/29)^{1/4}$ and their entropies differ while their stress-energy tensors agree. A separate causal-fluid example starts with identical sources and geometric data but different constitutive responses; the two models' curvature histories separate at linear order in proper time and their scale factors at cubic order. For black hole candidates, the relevant distinction is between stationary exterior parameters, perturbing fluxes and constituent history. The framework provides a test for whether retained data identify a material property, separating instantaneous source equality, history-wide source equality and observational projection.
title: Curvature Blindness: Material Inference in Stars and Black Hole Candidates

summary: We consider three-dimensional imaging of compactly supported anisotropic electric media from fixed-frequency polarimetric Maxwell far-field data. Maxwell transversality creates an obstruction absent from scalar Born inversion: each measurement determines only a projected action of the tensor-valued Fourier transform. We first resolve this obstruction by a finite-dimensional polarimetric inversion. For a general complex $3\times3$ contrast, three incidence--observation configurations are necessary, and we give an explicit three-configuration design that is sufficient at every nonzero interior Fourier point. Its Gram determinant yields quantitative conditioning information and exhibits the loss of recoverability at the boundary of the accessible Fourier ball. After tensor demixing, the inverse problem reduces componentwise to restricted Fourier inversion on the unit ball, which we regularize by spectral cutoff in three-dimensional ball generalized prolate spheroidal wave functions. For discrete acquisition, a combined reconstruction error estimate separates the effects of measurement noise, polarimetric amplification, off-grid Fourier mismatch, quadrature error, Born modeling error, and spectral truncation. Numerical tests examine polarimetric conditioning and use analytically generated Born data to compare three- and six-configuration recovery and assess off-grid sensitivity. Reconstructions from full-Maxwell volume-integral data assess the effects of noise, wavenumber, and basis choice, as well as the recovery of different tensor components.
title: Polarimetric Low-Rank Imaging of Anisotropic Maxwell Media

summary: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.
title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI

summary: PHOTOSTABILITY OF BOTANICAL ACTIVES AND PACKAGING ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT 中文書名:植物活性成分光穩定性與包材工程極限 Photostability of Botanical Actives and Packaging Engineering at the Limit is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating three coupled but independently falsifiable questions: photochemical degradation of identifiable botanical marker compounds, wavelength-resolved optical transmission through real packaging, and the qualification of storage safety against oxygen ingress and unknown photoproducts. Its central claim is conditional, not asserted. A package that retains more apparent active compound after simulated light exposure may simply exclude oxygen, reduce lamp heating, alter extraction recovery, or hide degradation products. The proposed test therefore crosses films with matched oxygen-transmission rates but contrasting spectral transmittance, and films with matched optical protection but contrasting oxygen transport. Incident spectra, absorbed dose, headspace oxygen, intact parent, isomers and degradants must remain distinct physical measurements. The opening candidate relation D_light = integral over time and wavelength of E_lambda times A_lambda formalizes spectral exposure only within explicitly measured optical and unit conventions. Thirty mathematically diverse research plates specify physical construction, dimensions, assumptions, blind falsification and linked chapters. Eighty-two research chapters and 410 separate-page investigations explore botanical provenance, optical metrology, photochemistry, oxygen transport, package manufacture, chemical recovery, second-site requalification and governance of false-positive claims. Two hundred single-page Research Gates challenge identifiable observables and strong alternative explanations; thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos describe distinguishable scientific instruments, assay references, failure sentinels, and research inheritance objects. Each Gate preserves an adverse test and a successor handoff rather than presuming the hypothesis will win. Three author-designated STARLI mother works provide methodological ancestry in identity protection, functional requalification and uncertainty-aware sampling, not experimental evidence of this skincare application. External method references span IUPAC actinometry, ASTM optical transmission and oxygen permeation, curcumin and anthocyanin photochemistry, and barrier-film research. Their scientific domains and limits are explicitly differentiated. This manuscript is a prospective, nonclinical Research Working Edition, not a completed photostability campaign, human trial, proof of cosmetic efficacy, or regulatory approval. Author: Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli Series: STARLI Research Institute XXXV / Herbal Nano-Quantum Skincare Atlas / Flagship F22

summary: BIOLOGICAL SAMPLE MICROSCALE ISOLATION AND ANTI-CROSS-CONTAMINATION AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:生物樣本微尺度隔離與防交叉污染極限 BIOLOGICAL SAMPLE MICROSCALE ISOLATION AND ANTI-CROSS-CONTAMINATION AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page, high-density English research monograph on whether microrobotic microscale isolation can improve sample-identity probability while limiting contact impulse, carryover and rare-sample loss. Its central claim is deliberately falsifiable. Under equal sample, time, energy, photon and analysis budgets, a preregistered isolation architecture should improve sample-identity probability without worsening contact impulse or carryover relative to commercial fluorescence-activated sorting at equal sample budget. A favorable result is rejected if downstream sensing creates the apparent improvement, rare targets silently disappear, purity rises by discarding difficult events, surface residue remains unresolved, or recovery improves while viability or molecular integrity fails. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates develop coverage entropy, calibrated identity posteriors, carryover transition models, complete material balance, rare-cell recovery and loss, purity, surface-memory decay, adsorption, desorption kinetics, hydrodynamic regime checks, contact impulse, shear dose, collision hazard, viability and molecular-integrity retention, blank limits, detection limits, witness information, uncertainty, equal-budget FACS effects, cross-site concordance and conjunctive release. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the book moves from identity authority and spatial coverage through contamination memory, microscale material closure, microrobotic contact physics, rare-cell accounting, decontamination, sample integrity, commercial FACS comparison and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates carry unique titles, questions, perturbations, rival accounts and evidence packets. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose genuinely different scientific objects, including contamination-memory ledgers, rare-cell censuses, adsorption compasses, waste-stream beacons, delayed-viability clocks and failure-preserving successor seeds. The work is explicitly nonclinical and hypothesis-generating. It does not claim clinical efficacy, regulatory approval or autonomous in-body deployment. Recovery improvement accompanied by failed viability or molecular integrity is a hard stop. No weighted score may compensate for broken identity, carryover beyond the preregistered ceiling or an unresolved material-balance residual. summary: Next-generation smart sensing devices necessitate on-chip integration of power-efficient reference circuits. The latters are required to provide other circuit blocks with highly reliable bias signals, even in the presence of temperature shifts and supply voltage disturbances, while draining a small fraction of the overall power budget. In particular, it is especially challenging to design current references with enhanced robustness and efficiency; hence, thorough exploration of novel architectures and design approaches is needed for this type of circuits. In this work, we propose a novel CMOS-only current reference, achieving temperature compensation by exploiting geometry dependences of the threshold voltage (specifically, the reverse short-channel effect and the narrow-channel effect). This allows reaching first-order temperature compensation within a single current reference core. Implemented in 0.18 μm CMOS, a version of the proposed current reference designed to deliver 141 nA (with 377 nW of total power consumption) achieved an average temperature coefficient equal to 194 ppm/°C (from −20 °C to 80 °C) and an average line sensitivity of −0.017%/V across post-layout statistical Monte Carlo simulations. Based on such findings, the newly proposed design methodology stands out as a noteworthy solution to design robust current references for power-constrained mixed-signal systems-on-chip.
title: A CMOS Current Reference with Novel Temperature Compensation Based on Geometry-Dependent Threshold Voltage Effects

summary: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a complex condition involving bidirectional interactions between cardiovascular and renal dysfunction. Its pathophysiology includes hemodynamic abnormalities, venous congestion, neurohormonal activation, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and metabolic disturbances. This narrative review aims to analyze the mechanisms of CRS and assess the relationship between renal function and clinical prognosis in patients with cardiovascular diseases, focusing on mortality, heart failure hospitalization, kidney dysfunction progression, and treatment-related renal changes. The review synthesizes evidence from clinical guidelines, randomized trials, observational studies, and contemporary scientific publications, with particular attention to CRS classification, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), serum creatinine, albuminuria, biomarkers, and treatment outcomes. The evidence indicates that reduced eGFR, albuminuria, persistent congestion, and worsening renal function provide complementary prognostic information. An analysis of 3,715 EVEREST trial participants found that each 30% decline in eGFR was associated with an increased risk of death and cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization. The DOSE trial showed that intensive diuretic treatment could improve fluid removal and symptoms while increasing short-term creatinine elevations. These findings highlight the importance of interpreting renal function changes alongside congestion, hemodynamic stability, baseline kidney function, and treatment response. Comprehensive cardiorenal risk assessment should incorporate renal function, albuminuria, urine output, cardiac biomarkers, electrolyte status, and clinical response to treatment. Further prospective studies are needed to validate integrated risk models in diverse patient populations.

summary: CAR-T therapy is a powerful treatment for pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). However, the impact of bridging therapy prior to CAR-T infusion on patient outcomes remains insufficiently explored. In this retrospective study of patients with relapse/refractory B-ALL (N = 103), we compared outcomes across different bridging therapy groups: Low-Intensity Chemotherapy (LIC, N = 50), Immunotherapy (N = 20), or High-Intensity Chemotherapy (HIC, N = 33). At day +28 post-infusion, LIC and Immunotherapy showed significantly higher rates of Complete Remission with negative Minimal Residual Disease compared with HIC (96% vs 85% vs 75%), along with lower rates of disease progression (4% vs 10% vs 15.2%) and treatment-related mortality (0% vs 5% vs 9.1%). Additionally, patients who received three or more prior lines of therapy before CAR-T infusion exhibited significantly lower response rates. Despite potential biases, such as intrinsic disease aggressiveness or unidentified genomic alterations, present findings suggest that using LIC or immunotherapy as bridging strategies, in patients with fewer prior treatment lines, may be associated with a lower overall disease and treatment burden and could potentially contribute to improved CAR-T cell efficacy and clinical outcomes. Nevertheless, additional investigations are required to elucidate biological and clinical mechanisms by which bridging approaches and treatment history modulate CAR-T responses. summary: The Duty-Primacy Test: Measuring the Operational Completeness of Algorithmic Transparency Registers (v3, Extended Empirical Edition) Oct 30, 2026 · @craig davidson ABSTRACT Public registers often fail to provide actionable accountability regarding automated tools, lacking clear duty-bearers, failure safeguards, or challenge mechanisms. summary: An open benchmark for testing geochemical fertility indices for magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE sulfide deposits. The benchmark contains 13,025 whole-rock analyses from 514 mafic-ultramafic intrusions labeled fertile, weakly mineralized, or barren, together with sample-type classifications, a reproducible scoring workflow, and a public leaderboard. Preprint: Danso, B.K., Dankwa, J.O., Aidoo, A.A. (2026). Fertile or Barren: an open benchmark for testing geochemical fertility indices on mineralized and barren mafic-ultramafic intrusions. Preprint, not peer reviewed; submitted to EarthArXiv. Included in this record as Danso_et_al_2026_Fertile_or_Barren_preprint.pdf. Version 0.1.1: adds the preprint and Figure 1b (benchmark intrusions in the conterminous United States, with USGS deposits). Data, labels and leaderboard scores are unchanged from v0.1.0. Headline numbers: 34 fertile, 19 weakly mineralized and 461 barren intrusions. Best index: Pd/Ir, AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.62-0.85). Three indices rank barren intrusions above fertile ones (Ni/Cu, Ni depletion vs MgO, Cu/Zr). Contents: benchmark table (data/processed/benchmark_samples.csv); intrusion table with labels, deposits and references (data/processed/intrusions.csv, data/curated/); public scoring program (code/score.py); leaderboard of 12 indices (leaderboard/); figures and tables (paper/); pipeline that rebuilds everything from the public sources (run_all.sh); codebook, scoring rules, limitations and verification record (docs/). Sources: GEOROC precompiled compilations (DIGIS Team, GRO.data, September 2026, CC BY-SA 4.0); USGS Critical Mineral Deposits of the United States ver. 3.0; USGS magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE inventory (2026); USGS Mineral Resources Data System. Please also cite GEOROC and the original sample publications (GEOROC reference numbers in the CITATIONS column). Licenses: data CC BY-SA 4.0; code MIT; figures and tables CC BY 4.0. summary: This dataset contains the supplementary material to the article “Adaptive Event Disambiguation via Alignments with Deferred Decisions” , submitted to the journal Process Science. datasets/ : the two synthetically generated datasets used in the evaluation, each in its own folder ( blood_donation , smart_home ). Each folder contains: runs.txt : the normative process behavior as a set of reference runs (one run per line), i.e. the model log against which traces are aligned. Activities are encoded as single symbols. labels.json : the mapping between activity labels and the symbols used in runs.txt . ambiguous.xes : the ambiguous event log, i.e. a set of traces in which events affected by ambiguity carry all their competing candidate activity labels. gold_standard.xes : the corresponding unambiguous log, used as ground truth for measuring disambiguation accuracy. Each log describes 15,000 executions of a process: Blood donation (BD): a blood-donation process synthesized from 32 real executions in an IoT-augmented lab setup. Smart home (SH): a smart-home process derived from the BP-Meets-IoT 2020 challenge dataset ( details ) by filtering for kitchen/eating-routine activities and discovering a model with the inductive miner. The sets of mutually ambiguous activities are {Check blood drawing machine, Take out samples} and {Disinfect injection site, Apply tourniquet, Insert needle, Remove tourniquet, Remove needle} for BD, and {Go fridge, Go dining table} , {Get cold warm food, Go kitchen shelf, Get food from fridge} , {Go micro, Get bread} for SH. The generated traces are stochastically perturbed to reflect IoT-based monitoring imperfections: process events are randomly skipped (simulating activities undetected by the IoT setup), and, for the healthcare scenario, additional hand hygiene events are inserted at random points (reflecting their unpredictable occurrence). Perturbation uses Java’s java.util.Random without a fixed seed, so each released log is one concrete instantiation of this stochastic process; the resulting traces may be non-conforming to the normative behavior. The third dataset used in the paper, HR recruitment (HR) , is a publicly available uncertain event log and is not redistributed here; it is available at its original repository (description: HaifaUniversityBPM/traffic-data-to-event-log ). Only its evaluation results are included (see below). results/ : the evaluation results for all three datasets ( X ∈ { BD , SH , HR }), one workbook per algorithm configuration: X_adaptive.xlsx : the adaptive algorithm (ABD in the paper). X_maxk_y.xlsx : the fixed-bound algorithm (FBD) with exploration bound maxK = y , for y = 1..5 . X_baseline.xlsx : the random-choice null-model baseline (RND), which has no access to the reference behavior and selects uniformly among the candidate labels of each ambiguous event. The random choice uses a fixed seed for reproducibility. Each workbook reports disambiguation quality and runtime for that configuration, organized into the following sheets: Summary : headline figures: dataset, algorithm (and maxK for FBD), number of events and traces, all-events disambiguation accuracy, mean fitness of the gold-standard and of the disambiguated traces, mean fitness drop, and mean runtime (per trace and per event). AllEvents : one row per event comparing the gold-standard label with the disambiguated label ( Are equal ); the basis of the all-events accuracy. Results : per-trace accuracy (total events, number of mismatches, accuracy). Fitness : per-case fitness of the gold-standard and disambiguated traces (run/trace length, synchronous and asynchronous moves, fitness) and the per-case fitness drop. Runtime_Ambiguous : per-trace runtime (ms) on the input log, with one column per measurement repeat and the average. The source code implementing the fixed-bound and adaptive algorithms is available in this GitHub repository .
title: Adaptive Event Disambiguation via Alignments with Deferred Decisions

summary: 🌟 Summary Ultralytics 8.4.194 makes automatic batch sizing more reliable across tasks, alongside practical fixes for model loading, results saving, datasets, and deployment workflows. 📊 Key Changes 🚀 Automatic batch sizing now uses the training dataset for every task. It accounts for dataset size and labels across classification, detection, and multi-dataset training. If profiling runs out of memory during backward computation, AutoBatch treats that as a limit rather than relying on an invalid measurement. 🛡️ Model YAML parsing is safer and more consistent. Activations must resolve to supported torch.nn modules, and model entries must be PyTorch module classes. Custom YAMLs using other expressions may need updating. 💾 Saving prediction results is more robust. Results.save() and plot(save=True) now produce sensible .jpg filenames for sources such as webcams, videos, or missing paths, and create parent directories when needed. 🔄 Similarity search uses the selected image directory on each startup. This avoids reusing stale indexes from another dataset; the trade-off is that embeddings are rebuilt each time. 🧩 Dataset and URL handling is more dependable. Non-PNG semantic masks are resolved before cache hashing, and URL schemes such as HTTPS:// , GS:// , and UL:// are now handled without case sensitivity. 📈 Benchmarking and evaluation guidance are clearer. TensorFlow GraphDef benchmarks now include OBB and pose, and the docs explain that classes absent from validation receive the overall mAP value rather than a measured per-class score. 🎯 Purpose & Impact ✅ AutoBatch is less likely to choose a batch size that exceeds a small dataset or available GPU memory, and multi-dataset World/YOLOE training avoids label-access failures. 🔒 Consistent, restricted YAML parsing improves safety, though nonstandard custom model configurations may no longer load. 🧰 More reliable result saving, mask-cache updates, and URL routing reduce common workflow errors. 🔍 Similarity search results better reflect the images currently in the chosen folder, while requiring index-building work at startup. 📚 Documentation updates clarify metric interpretation and integration behavior; no new model architecture is introduced in this release. summary: 智能機器人物質驅動的自主底盤極限 13/90 ROBOTIC-MATTER-DRIVEN AUTONOMOUS CHASSIS AT THE LIMIT ROBOTIC-MATTER-DRIVEN AUTONOMOUS CHASSIS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page high-density English research working monograph examining whether a chassis made from interacting robotic-matter modules can reversibly change its load-bearing geometry without losing structural integrity, traction confidence, actuator authority or independently reconstructable state identity. Its scope is limited to unoccupied, scaled rigs and falsifiable engineering research. Its principal hypothesis can be refuted. With equivalent materials, mass, testing time, energy, sensing and control resources, a preregistered adaptive chassis should improve traction reserve without worsening energy per mission, path error, or structural stability relative to a well-tuned fixed-geometry chassis and conservative rule-based controller. Apparent gains that vanish under actuator, controller or load-path ablations cannot be attributed to robotic matter. Thirty mathematical and physical research plates address six-degree dynamic balance, graph rigidity, stiffness and failure modes, contact-force closure, structural interface stress, fatigue, consensus, latency, support margins, power accounting, sensor covariance, fault identification and noncompensatory release. Each plate defines units, validity assumptions, an independent physical counter-test and links to substantive chapter investigations. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the volume develops mechanical architectures, connector physics, reversible stiffness, decentralized actuation, ground interaction, reference metrology, energy integrity, wear, fair baselines and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates frame specific blinded perturbations, rival explanations and hard stopping conditions. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct tools, diagnostic instruments and successor-ready verification interfaces. This book is hypothesis-generating. It does not report a completed STARLI chassis experiment, nanoscale vehicle manufacturing, quantum superiority or passenger-safe operation. Unknown traction, unstable support, unverifiable mechanical locking, reference invalidity or revoked physical authority require stopping and withholding conclusions. Competing laboratories are invited to reproduce, refute and improve the proposals while keeping failed experiments visible. summary: This dataset contains regional candidate insect species checklists and supporting occurrence records for the Jack and Laura Dangermond Preserve, California. The checklists identify species recorded in EPA ecoregions intersecting the preserve. They provide a regional reference for biodiversity inventory and survey planning; inclusion does not confirm occurrence on the preserve. Contents Original GBIF Darwin Core Archive containing 4,665,086 California Arthropoda records. Four species checklists covering EPA Level III ecoregions 6 and 85 and Level IV ecoregions 6ap and 85a. Checklist column definitions. Two supporting occurrence tables: 1,408,875 Level III records and 43,555 Level IV records. The combined Level III checklists contain 13,634 species ; the combined Level IV checklists contain 2,550 species . Lists overlap, and the Level IV occurrence table is a subset of the Level III table. Methods Records were filtered to usable coordinates, insects and the selected ecoregions, followed by species-level identification and taxonomic resolution. Names were matched using the GBIF Species Match API v2 with Catalogue of Life eXtended Release, supplemented by project-reviewed corrections. Subspecies were grouped under species for checklist summaries. Common names were obtained from the Entomological Society of America. Each checklist includes common name, order, family, resolved scientific name, regional occurrence count and documented preserve occurrence. Preserve-occurrence flags also draw on the UCSB Summer 2026 survey and a separate GBIF preserve extract. These additional sources are not included in this deposit. Interpretation and limitations Occurrence counts represent records, not individuals. A blank preserve-occurrence flag means occurrence was not documented in the sources examined, rather than confirmed absence. Candidate lists were not filtered by habitat or vegetation and do not assign occurrence probabilities. The current snapshot retains five Level III absence records, including one in Level IV, and a Level III scorpion classification requiring review. Consult the README for further limitations. Source and reuse GBIF.org. (2026, September 28). GBIF occurrence download . https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.vgv5ee Source records retain their individual licenses and attribution requirements. Methods, code and supporting documentation are available at: https://github.com/cheadle-biodiversity/Dangermond-arthropods Document Provenance and AI Assistance Statement Documentation and workflow development received AI assistance through Codex. Researchers remain responsible for scientific review, taxonomic decisions and publication approval.

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow.
